## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a robot pass every trial and still lack the evidence needed for deployment?_

A robot that repeatedly opens one door has supplied evidence about that door, its own hardware, and the conditions of those trials. It has not established how it will behave at a displaced latch, with a different payload, or after its sensors drift. Its admitted actions also change the observations it receives, so agreement with recorded demonstrations cannot substitute for testing the resulting motion. Physical trials expose that feedback, but each consumes time and mechanical life, and protective interventions stop some trajectories before their consequences unfold. Evaluation must therefore connect the task outcome to the conditions sampled, preserve every intervention, and state the uncertainty that remains. Its product is a bounded claim about the learned proposer, together with the uncovered conditions the rest of the machine must address. Because actions cross an irreversible causal boundary, evidence of policy competence must remain distinct from permission to move.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Interpret physical success rates as conditional evidence about a specified machine, environment, and trial protocol
- Compare open-loop prediction accuracy with closed-loop behavior shaped by the policy's own actions
- Select the evidence regime (replay, simulation, shadow operation, or constrained physical testing) that can answer a given evaluation question
- Calculate confidence bounds, trial counts, and test time for a zero-failure campaign under stated sampling assumptions
- Interpret completion and intervention metrics without crediting the policy for protection supplied by its supervision
- Diagnose how hardware differences, environmental changes, and stopping rules alter the claim a campaign can support
- Evaluate which rare failures remain unsupported by feasible testing and the available statistical assumptions
- Design a predeclared trial protocol with fixed outcome rules and full-denominator accounting of interventions and aborts
- Construct an evaluation record that bounds its operational claim and identifies coverage gaps and required protections

:::

## The Door Campaign {#sec-evaluation-door-campaign}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DOOR CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: chapter opener, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the lease fallacy.
# │ Show: the evaluated campaign (latch task, base stopped) and the machine
# │       values the chapter quotes: approach speed, tripwire, latch limit, rack
# │       capacity, chunk period, and chunk lease; plus the Part II funnel
# │       the completed record carries (ledger cells, supported cells,
# │       known absences, manifest omissions).
# │ How: registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle;
# │      the standoff and the ledger counts (from @sec-data and
# │      @sec-training) are chapter-local inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_frequency, check, MarkdownStr

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EvalMachine:
    """The latch campaign Ch7 evaluates, on the book's running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    standoff = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; base start distance from the door
    v_approach = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative; guarded approach, the declared ODD's speed
    f_latch_limit = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative; latch damage limit
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative; contact tripwire that ends an attempt (@sec-data)
    rack_capacity = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen; tote-rack capacity
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk policy rate
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease
    n_plate_positions = 3  # category: illustrative; nominal and two displaced plates, the scenario ledger of @sec-data
    ledger_speeds = [AISLE.v_latch_approach, AISLE.v_latch_high]  # category: illustrative; the ledger's two approach speeds
    n_supported = 1  # category: illustrative; the nominal plate at the guarded approach (LatchScenarioLedger in @sec-data)
    n_omissions = 2  # category: illustrative; soft penalty contact and missing transport lag, the manifest's omission log

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    n_speeds = len(ledger_speeds)
    n_cells = n_plate_positions * n_speeds
    n_absences = n_cells - n_supported

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_approach.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded approach is not 0.03 m/s")
    check(abs(f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit is not 100 N")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Contact tripwire is not 15 N")
    check(f_trip < f_latch_limit, "The tripwire must end an attempt well below the damage limit")
    check(abs(rack_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is not 50 kg")
    check(abs(chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk period is not 50 ms")
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is not 60 ms")
    check(chunk_period < t_lease, "Chunk period must fit inside the lease")
    check(n_cells == 6 and n_supported == 1 and n_absences == 5, "Ledger should have one supported cell of six (matches @sec-data)")
    check(n_omissions == 2, "Manifest omission log holds two unclosed departures (matches @sec-training)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    standoff_str = fmt_length(standoff, precision=0)
    v_approach_str = fmt_velocity(v_approach, precision=2)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    rack_capacity_str = fmt_mass(rack_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease)
    _words = {1: "one", 2: "two", 3: "three", 5: "five", 6: "six"}
    n_plate_positions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_plate_positions])
    n_speeds_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_speeds])
    n_cells_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_cells])
    n_supported_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_supported])
    n_absences_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_absences])
    n_omissions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_omissions])
```

Fresh from the offline training pipeline, `latch-bc-01` is flashed onto the warehouse mobile manipulator; it is the checkpoint admitted by the original policy manifest in @sec-training-policy-manifest for this nominal campaign. In the illustrative initial validation campaign, suppose the machine completes twenty consecutive runs of its door task. Each run starts with the base `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide) from the spring-latched cage door; the base drives in and stops, and with the base at rest the arm unlatches and opens the door at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, without a contact-tripwire crossing or a human intervention. Its empirical sample success rate is $\hat{p} = 1.00$ (100 percent). In static machine learning benchmarks, scoring $\hat{p} = 1.00$ across an evaluation batch is often celebrated as an empirical triumph. In physical AI systems engineering, that record leaves the deployment decision unresolved, because twenty clean runs establish only a bounded statistical lower limit and leave substantial uncertainty about unobserved failures.

The campaign needs an outcome rule and a sampled population before its perfect observed fraction can be interpreted. The same record must distinguish what the learned policy accomplished from what supervision supplied.

## Metric Coverage and Limitations of Scalar Success Rates {#sec-evaluation-what-measured}

The same latch policy can open the nominal door and jam against a displaced strike plate. Its measured success rate therefore belongs to the coupled policy, mechanical plant, computational hardware, environment, and trial protocol. Even a reproducible offline score describes a model on a specified dataset, not its behavior under arbitrary conditions.

The **offline evaluation illusion** is the mistaken belief that lower validation loss, higher action cosine similarity, or smaller Mean Squared Error (MSE) on logged data establishes superior physical performance. Offline loss functions $\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \|a_i^* - \pi_\theta(s_i^*)\|^2$ score predictions along frozen demonstrator trajectories. Physical evaluation must instead specify the conditions under which admitted actions generate the next state.

To evaluate a policy, an engineering team executes a sequence of discrete physical runs. A single trial is fully determined only when every variable that can alter the physical state trajectory is fixed or explicitly sampled. Formally, let a single trial condition be defined by a tuple $c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa)$, drawn from an operational testing distribution $\mathcal{D}$. The vector $s_0$ represents the initial state of the machine, including pose in the Special Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$\index{SE(3) pose} (three-dimensional position and orientation), linear and angular velocities, and joint encoder positions. The environment vector $e$ captures external variables such as floor friction ($\mu$), ambient illuminance, obstacle geometry, and ambient air temperature. The machine state $m$ captures physical and hardware properties drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, encompassing unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances, battery state of charge, payload mass, tire wear, mechanical backlash\index{Mechanical backlash} in harmonic drive gearboxes, and sensor calibration matrices. The computational configuration $\pi_\theta$ encompasses the frozen policy weights $\theta$, inference quantization, scheduling deadlines, and software versions. Finally, the termination protocol $\kappa = (T_{\max}, g, \phi)$ defines the execution time limit $T_{\max}$, the spatial goal region $g$, and the binary evaluation function $\phi$ that maps the resulting trajectory to a terminal outcome $Y \in \{0, 1\}$.

In static machine learning benchmarks, inputs $(x_i, y_i)$ are sampled independently from a static data distribution $p_{\text{data}}(x, y)$. In Physical AI, the continuous trajectory $\text{Traj}(c) = (s_0, u_0, s_1, u_1, \dots, s_T)$ is generated sequentially by the closed-loop physical state transition kernel:
$$s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{T}(s_t, u_t; m, e), \quad a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t), \quad u_t = \text{Gate}(a_t, s_t)$$
The true success probability under this evaluation protocol is the expected value of the binary task outcome averaged over the joint distribution of trial conditions:
$$p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$$
(@sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution gives the formal integral). In test engineering, the abstract distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is operationalized through a **stratified test matrix** or Latin hypercube sampling grid across controllable parameters—systematically varying payload mass, approach speed, illumination, and initial spatial standoff—while logging uncontrollable environmental parameters such as ambient temperature and floor friction. Unstratified, naive random sampling is inadequate because it oversamples benign nominal states while leaving boundary regions unvisited.

Here $\text{Traj}(c)$ is the physical trajectory generated under condition $c$. Changing floor friction or battery voltage changes the transition kernel $\mathcal{T}$ even with identical weights $\theta$. The sampling protocol is consequently part of the quantity being estimated.

::: {#dfn-evaluation-closed-loop-estimand .callout-definition title="Closed-loop evaluation estimand"}

***Closed-loop evaluation estimand***\index{Closed-loop evaluation estimand!definition}\index{Evaluation estimand!definition} is the expected physical task outcome $p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$ defined over the joint distribution of initial states, mechanical plant wear, environmental physics, frozen policy weights, and evaluation predicates:
$$c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa) \sim \mathcal{D}$$
rather than an intrinsic property of the neural policy weights evaluated in isolation.

1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is treated as a property of the model $\pi_\theta$. In physical AI, substituting a worn tire, letting battery voltage sag, or shifting ambient illuminance alters the physical state transition function without changing a single weight. The sampling distribution of operational conditions $\mathcal{D}$ is an inseparable part of the quantity being estimated.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike open-loop validation metrics (such as validation loss, cosine similarity, or mean squared trajectory error) which score predictions against frozen recorded states, the closed-loop estimand integrates over the endogenous feedback loop where past actions physically move the machine, directly changing the future sensor observations it will receive.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reporting a single success rate percentage without predeclaring the support, density, and environmental bounds of the test distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Any physical policy can be made arbitrarily successful by testing exclusively in benign, unperturbed states.

:::

### Hardware instance variance and environmental unobservables

The physical mechanisms that alter $c$ between trials operate independently of the policy, and the mobile manipulator exhibits each of them across two major sources of dispersion: **hardware instance variance** and **environmental unobservables**.

First, hardware instance variance reflects the physical reality that robotic production lines do not manufacture identical copies. Even within the same manufacturing batch, robots exhibit unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances:

- **Gearbox backlash and compliance**: Harmonic drive gearboxes in the arm exhibit machining tolerances resulting in joint backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$). Under direction reversals, this deadband introduces non-linear hysteresis and phase lag that destabilize tight neural feedback loops.
- **Structural link compliance**: Elastic link deflection under payload varies across chassis assemblies, shifting the true Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool center point} relative to forward kinematics calculations.
- **Sensor assembly misalignments**: Real-world camera mounts and depth sensor brackets deviate by $\pm 1\text{ to }3\text{ mm}$ and $\pm 0.5^\circ$ from CAD nominals, introducing systematic coordinate frame offsets between sensor frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{cam}}$ and base frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{base}}$.
- **Actuator electrical variance**: Motor phase resistances and torque constants ($K_t$) vary by up to $\pm 5$ percent across stator windings. Furthermore, as the battery discharges\index{State of charge (SoC)}, the drives lose voltage headroom against back-electromotive force (back-EMF)\index{Back-EMF}, shifting the torque-speed curve\index{Torque-speed curve} and diminishing acceleration authority.

Second, environmental unobservables alter the physical interaction dynamics without changing camera pixels in a way the neural network recognizes. Ambient daylight shifting across the warehouse alters illuminance, causing camera auto-exposure to stretch shutter times, inducing motion blur during base turns. Direct solar glare at dawn or dusk saturates complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor arrays, washing out visual contrast at the latch interface. On the floor, dust accumulation and ambient humidity alter the tire-floor friction coefficient ($\mu$), extending braking distance. In the manipulator arm, repeated door openings generate Joule heating ($I^2 R$)\index{Joule heating} in motor windings and warm harmonic drive lubricants, decreasing damping and expanding link dimensions. Consequently, the tool-center point meets the latch at a different spatial offset on a hot afternoon than on a cold morning. A policy evaluated across twenty trials on Unit 01 in the morning may fail completely when tested on Unit 02 in the afternoon, despite running identical frozen weights.

The reset procedure moves $c$ as well. An operator who repositions the base after a difficult run may favor an easy start, and an automated reset that repeats one path heats the windings cyclically. An operator who catches a failing run and discards it as a reset erases the hardest failure from the sample. Statistical evaluation must therefore distinguish sampling variation from a change in the estimand. When $n$ trials are drawn from a fixed $\mathcal{D}$, the sample proportion $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$ fluctuates around $p(\mathcal{D})$, and standard estimators bound that noise. Loading the tote rack or moving the door's strike plate changes the experiment to a different distribution $\mathcal{D}'$ with its own $p(\mathcal{D}')$, and pooling the two samples combines observations from two different machines.

### Intervention-based physical metrics

A door may open after the permission path slightly reduces the proposed force. That run can satisfy the whole-machine service requirement while exposing a limitation of the raw proposer. A stop short of the door can instead preserve the physical limit while failing the task. A human recovery can complete the task without demonstrating unassisted autonomy. These outcomes require separate fields.

We therefore report whole-machine task completion within its time and physical limits, raw proposer autonomy, and protective outcomes independently. Normal least-change adjustments remain part of the designed machine. They reduce the strict unassisted metric below, but do not automatically make a completed task a system failure. Intervention logs distinguish adjustments, rejected proposals, protective stops, and human takeovers, with a predeclared event-counting rule so a sustained clamp is not confused with many independent incidents.

1. **Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR)**: Let $I_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ be the total count of supervisory interventions (whether by human operators, runtime permission filters, or emergency tripwires) during trial $i$, and let $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote goal achievement within the time limit $T_{\max}$. The unassisted autonomous success indicator is defined as:
   $$A_i = \mathbb{I}(Y_i = 1 \land I_i = 0)$$
   The Autonomous Completion Rate is the sample proportion of completely unassisted trials:
   $$\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n A_i = \frac{N_{\text{unassisted}}}{n}$$
   ACR here measures strict raw proposer autonomy: even one recorded override gives $A_i = 0$. The separate task outcome $Y_i$ may still be one when normal filtering permits completion within the declared service limits.

2. **Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**: For a declared intervention class, MTBI measures its frequency during active execution:
   $$T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{T_{\text{active}}}{N_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n I_i}$$
   where $t_{\text{active}, i}$ is the active operating duration of trial $i$ and $N_{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i$ is the total number of recorded interventions. MTBI measures the burden of that event class. Frequent automatic adjustments and frequent human takeovers have different staffing consequences; neither this ratio nor zero observed damage establishes deployment readiness.

3. **Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$)**: In spatial navigation and continuous trajectory tracking, interventions must be normalized against physical exposure distance or discrete control steps:
   $$D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n L_i} \quad [\text{interventions per kilometer}] \quad \text{or} \quad D_{\text{int}} = 1{,}000 \times \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_{\text{steps}, i}} \quad [\text{interventions per } 1{,}000 \text{ steps}]$$
   where $L_i$ is the path distance traversed. Intervention density exposes whether policy degradation is uniformly distributed or concentrated at specific geometric bottlenecks (such as narrow doorway passages).

4. **Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)**: In physical qualification campaigns, the true experimental cost is governed by the time required to recover the plant and environment after a trial concludes or aborts:
   $$T_{\text{reset}} = t_{\text{physical\_restore}} + t_{\text{calibration}} + t_{\text{telemetry\_flush}}$$
   If a manipulation task takes 25 seconds of active execution ($t_{\text{run}} = 25\text{ s}$) but requires 60 seconds of manual reset latency ($T_{\text{reset}} = 60\text{ s}$) to clear jammed latch pins, recalibrate joint encoders, and return the base to its initial standoff, the reset latency consumes over 70 percent of test-cell occupancy. Campaigns with high reset latency create intense organizational pressure to take shortcuts—such as skipping motor thermal cooldown or repositioning the robot to easier initial poses—which corrupts trial stationarity.

::: {#dfn-evaluation-intervention-metrics .callout-definition title="Intervention-based physical metrics"}

***Intervention-based physical metrics***\index{Intervention-based physical metrics!definition}\index{Autonomous Completion Rate!definition}\index{Mean Time Between Interventions!definition}\index{Intervention Density!definition}\index{Reset Latency!definition} quantify autonomous policy performance through the frequency, spatial density, and recovery overhead of runtime safety overrides:

- **Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR)**: $\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(Y_i = 1 \land I_i = 0) = \frac{N_{\text{unassisted}}}{n}$, requiring zero overrides for unassisted success.
- **Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**: $T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{T_{\text{active}}}{N_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n I_i}$, measuring the burden of the declared intervention class.
- **Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$)**: $D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n L_i}$ or $1{,}000 \times \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_{\text{steps}, i}}$, reporting interventions per kilometer or per 1,000 discrete control steps.
- **Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)**: $T_{\text{reset}} = t_{\text{physical\_restore}} + t_{\text{calibration}} + t_{\text{telemetry\_flush}}$, tracking physical cell recovery downtime.
1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is a scalar score over frozen test samples. In physical AI, scalar success rates ($Y \in \{0, 1\}$) obscure policy inadequacy whenever runtime safety envelopes, Control Barrier Functions, or human safety operators intervene to prevent collisions. Zero hardware damage can coexist with frequent human takeover or automatic adjustment; event classes determine how that burden affects service.
2.  **Distinction**: Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) refers to a separately defined failure event, which need not be destruction. MTBI, ACR, and $D_{\text{int}}$ describe intervention burden and strict proposer autonomy inside the tested envelope. Conflating censored interventions with unassisted survival commits the censored trial fallacy.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Omitting Reset Latency from qualification budgets. When manual resets consume 70 percent of test-cell occupancy, operators face intense organizational pressure to bypass motor thermal cooldown periods or favor easier initial conditions, breaking trial stationarity.

:::

The outcome definitions identify what to count. The next choice is how to expose the feedback that can change those outcomes.

## Closed-Loop Dynamics {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics}

In standard deep learning pipelines, model performance is evaluated by computing empirical risk across a static held-out validation split $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)$$
Whether the target metric is Top-1 classification accuracy, token perplexity, F1 score, or action regression loss, evaluation is fundamentally passive and decoupled. The data-generating process is feedforward and memoryless with respect to the model's predictions: mispredicting sample $i$ has zero causal influence on sample $i+1$ ($\partial x_{i+1} / \partial \hat{y}_i = 0$). Relying on this static paradigm in embodied autonomy produces the **offline evaluation illusion**: the false assumption that minimizing regression loss or maximizing action cosine similarity against static logs translates to safe, stable closed-loop execution.

In Physical AI, this decoupling vanishes entirely. Actions cross the causal boundary into mass, momentum, and non-smooth contact mechanics. The policy's admitted actions physically move the plant, endogenously creating subsequent sensory inputs ($s_{t+1} = f(s_t, u_t)$). Actions are not classifications; they are physical forces, torques, and velocity setpoints that interact with inertia, friction, and backlash. A navigation policy can reproduce recorded aisle runs almost perfectly under static regression metrics, yet spend the base's entire clearance to a storage rack before traversing a third of the aisle. The difference lies in what each kind of test feeds back to the policy.

In an **open-loop evaluation**\index{Open-loop evaluation!definition}, a candidate policy $\pi_\theta$ is scored across a static dataset of recorded demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} = \{(s_t^*, a_t^*)\}_{t=1}^T$. At each discrete timestep $t$, the policy receives a recorded demonstrator state $s_t^*$ and outputs a predicted action $\hat{a}_t = \pi_\theta(s_t^*)$. An error metric, such as mean squared error or cross-entropy, measures the distance between $\hat{a}_t$ and the recorded expert action $a_t^*$. At step $t+1$, the evaluation pipeline supplies the next recorded state $s_{t+1}^*$ from the dataset. The action $\hat{a}_t$ produced by the policy is discarded without executing on hardware, keeping the sequence of input states independent of the policy's past outputs ($\partial s_{t+1}^* / \partial \hat{a}_t = 0$). In a **closed-loop evaluation**\index{Closed-loop evaluation!definition}, the policy proposes $a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t)$; the permission path checks it against measured state and constraints, applies $u_t$ (or a fallback), and the plant evolves as $s_{t+1} = f(s_t,u_t)$. The applied command changes the physical state and later observations, crossing the causal boundary in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}
*The Act $\rightarrow$ Sense feedback closure: actions physically perturb the environment, altering subsequent sensory observations.*
:::

### Compounding error and kinematic integration {#sec-evaluation-compounding-error}

Why does a neural policy that achieves negligible open-loop validation loss drive a physical robot off course within seconds? Open-loop evaluation tests actions exclusively along the demonstrator's static state trajectory, where inputs are forcibly reset to expert states at every clock cycle. In closed-loop deployment, because the policy's own admitted actions physically move the mechanical plant, small prediction errors immediately perturb subsequent sensor observations.

For a bounded illustration, let $\ell$ be the zero-one cost of disagreeing with a deterministic expert action, rather than an arbitrary regression loss. Assume its expectation is at most $\epsilon$ under the expert state distribution at each step of a $T$-step horizon, written $\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^*}[\ell(s, \pi_\theta(s))] \le \epsilon$. The expert's cumulative cost $J(\pi^*)$ is zero for this disagreement metric. On recorded expert states, the expected cumulative cost is bounded linearly:
$$\mathbb{E}_{\text{open}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \ell(s_t^*, \pi_\theta(s_t^*))\right] \le T \epsilon$$
In closed loop, the simplified transition $s_{t+1} = f(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t))$ includes the fixed permission path. Couple expert and candidate runs to the same initial state and disturbances; their states agree until the first differing action. A disagreement at step $t$ can then cost at most one at each remaining step. A union bound over possible first disagreements gives this worst-case imitation-cost bound [@ross2011reduction]:
$$\mathbb{E}_{\text{closed}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \ell(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t))\right] - J(\pi^*) \le \sum_{t=1}^T (T - t + 1)\epsilon = \mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$$
This bound does not apply directly to unbounded MSE, contact force, or damage severity. A separate kinematic calculation shows one physical consequence of persistent error: an uncorrected heading or steering bias integrates forward into macroscopic lateral displacement, causing the robot to exhaust its safe clearance envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEADING BIAS AGAINST THE AISLE'S SIDE CLEARANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Show: where a persistent 1 degree heading bias of the navigation stack
# │       (not the evaluated latch policy) spends the aisle's side clearance.
# │ How: y(t) = v sin(eps) t; t_impact = W_clear / (v sin(eps)); the side
# │      clearance is (aisle width - machine width) / 2.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_angle, fmt_math, sci_latex, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class AisleDrift:
    """Closed-loop drift of a biased navigation policy on the running machine's aisle."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative; side clearance each side
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    machine_width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative; base footprint
    heading_offset_deg = 1.0  # category: illustrative; persistent heading bias

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = math.radians(heading_offset_deg)
    eps_q = eps * radian
    angular_mse = (eps_q**2).to(radian**2)  # open-loop score on recorded centerline states
    t_impact = (clearance / (v * math.sin(eps))).to(ureg.second)
    x_impact = (v * t_impact).to(ureg.meter)
    aisle_fraction = (x_impact / aisle_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Side clearance is not 0.15 m")
    check(abs(((aisle_width - machine_width) / 2 - clearance).to(ureg.meter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Side clearance must equal (aisle - machine) / 2")
    check(abs(aisle_length.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, "Aisle length is not 30 m")
    check(abs(x_impact.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 8.6) < 0.05, "Clearance should be spent in about 8.6 m")
    check(abs(t_impact.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 5.73) < 0.005, "Clearance should be spent in about 5.7 s")
    check(aisle_fraction < 1 / 3, "Prose says less than a third of the aisle")
    check(abs(heading_offset_deg - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Prose, fig-cap, and fig-alt state a 1.0 degree heading offset")
    check(abs(angular_mse.magnitude - 3.05e-4) < 5e-7, "fig-alt states an angular MSE of 3.05e-4 rad^2")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, precision=2)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, precision=0)
    machine_width_str = fmt_length(machine_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    clearance_cm_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    t_impact_str = fmt_time(t_impact, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    x_impact_str = fmt_length(x_impact, precision=1)
    eps_rad_str = fmt_angle(eps_q, precision=5)
    angular_mse_math = fmt_math(rf"{sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
    angular_mse_eq = fmt_math(rf"\text{{MSE}}_\theta = ({fmt(eps, precision=5)})^2 \approx {sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
```

Open-loop evaluation tests actions along the demonstrator's state trajectory; a policy with low offline prediction error can fail when its biased proposals are admitted to physical motion, because its own actions carry it off the states it was trained on. This is the endogenous-data principle (\ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}); @sec-data-endogenous-experience developed its consequence for data, and evaluation must measure it on the machine. The door campaign cannot show the effect, because its base stands still while the arm works, so the example comes from the same machine's navigation stack rather than from the latch policy under evaluation. The base drives a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle at its `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit (both illustrative), and the nominal expert demonstration follows the centerline with heading $\theta^* = 0\text{ rad}$ and lateral offset $y^* = 0\text{ m}$. Suppose the candidate navigation policy has a systematic heading bias of $\epsilon_\theta = 1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) on every step, and the permission path admits each of these proposals because none is infeasible on its own while clearance remains.

In an open-loop evaluation, the policy receives the demonstrator state $s_t^* = (x_t^*, 0, 0)$ at each step and predicts a forward velocity with a $1.0^\circ$ steering offset. The offline scoring pipeline records a mean absolute angular error of $1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) and an extremely low mean squared error of `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_eq`.[^fn-math-openloop-mse] In closed-loop execution, however, because the machine physically moves based on previously admitted commands, uncorrected heading errors compound continuously over time. Under planar unicycle kinematics ($\dot{y} = v \sin \theta \approx v \epsilon_\theta$), a persistent angular offset integrates into a cumulative lateral displacement:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin \epsilon_\theta \, d\tau \approx v \epsilon_\theta t$$
If the policy exhibits a persistent yaw-rate bias $\omega_{\text{bias}}$ (steering drift) rather than a fixed heading offset, the heading angle itself grows linearly over time ($\theta(t) = \int_0^t \omega_{\text{bias}} \, d\tau = \omega_{\text{bias}} t$). Integrating forward velocity $v$ then produces a cumulative lateral excursion that compounds quadratically in time:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin(\omega_{\text{bias}} \tau) \, d\tau \approx \frac{1}{2} v \omega_{\text{bias}} t^2$$
Quadratic kinematic drift and the worst-case imitation-cost bound describe different quantities. The first integrates a persistent yaw-rate bias; the second bounds accumulated decision cost under distribution shift. Neither establishes exponential instability.

For the constant $1.0^\circ$ heading bias, the base is `{python} AisleDrift.machine_width_str` wide in a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_width_str` aisle, which leaves $W_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str` of side clearance to the rack on each side, and the drift spends that clearance at
$$t_{\text{impact}} = \frac{W_{\text{clear}}}{v \sin \epsilon_\theta},$$
which at the drive limit is `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str`, after `{python} AisleDrift.x_impact_str` of travel and less than a third of the way down the aisle (@fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop).[^fn-math-closedloop-lateral] Either the permission path's clearance check stops the base short of the rack or, without that check, the base strikes it. Both outcomes are a failed trial that open-loop scoring rated near-perfect.

[^fn-math-openloop-mse]: **Metric scale masking in regression loss**\index{Evaluation!metric masking}: Aggregating squared steering errors across thousands of validation frames obscures severe, intermittent directional mistakes. A single localized prediction spike of $15^\circ$ is mathematically washed out when averaged across hours of straight aisle driving. A brief angular spike can matter if its integrated motion exhausts clearance before the independent permission path responds; the outcome requires a plant and timing model.

[^fn-math-closedloop-lateral]: **Kinematic integration of heading bias**\index{Kinematics!lateral trajectory drift}: Holding heading at a constant $1.0^\circ$ offset produces linear lateral drift $y(t) = v \sin(\epsilon_\theta) t$. When steering rate is biased, unmitigated yaw integration yields quadratic drift $y(t) \approx \tfrac{1}{2} v \omega t^2$, accelerating impact with side racking.

::: {#psp-evaluation-open-loop-blindness .callout-perspective title="The offline evaluation illusion"}
Offline validation loss, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and action cosine similarity score predictions along frozen demonstrator trajectories where errors are erased at every clock cycle. Closed-loop tests expose accumulated displacement and states absent from the recordings. The worst-case imitation-cost bound ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$) does not prescribe a universal physical drift rate, while a local stiffness model ($F = k \Delta x$) explains why contact errors require their own force measurements. Evaluating tensor mimicry offline is blind to the causal feedback loop of physical autonomy.
:::

The aisle example shows both reasons that an open-loop score\index{Open-loop evaluation!closed-loop gap} decouples from closed-loop survival. First, static evaluation cannot integrate a persistent error into displacement. It resets the machine to an expert state at every clock cycle, masking the compounding of integration errors, whereas in closed loop the state at index $t$ is the expanded composition of all previous actions:
$$s_t = f(f(\dots f(s_0, u_0)\dots, u_{t-2}), u_{t-1})$$
A persistent heading bias needs no software bug, since differential tire wear, camera-mast vibration, or floor camber produces one. Second, static evaluation cannot follow the machine into the unfamiliar states that early errors steer it toward. The first admitted error moves the base from the demonstrated state $s_1^*$ to an unvisited state $s_1$, and once it drifts a few centimeters off the centerline it occupies states absent from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}$. The offline metric, computed only where $y = 0\text{ m}$, holds no evidence about $\pi_\theta(s)$ for $y \neq 0\text{ m}$, and a policy never shown recoveries from off-center states can make larger errors there, accelerating the divergence that @sec-training-synthesis-regimes traced for behavioral cloning.

### Contact discontinuities and metric masking {#sec-evaluation-non-lipschitz-contact}

Touching the latch can change motion abruptly: a gripper moving freely can strike the plate, stick, or slip. Ideal rigid-body models represent impacts as velocity jumps ($v^+ \ne v^-$) and static friction as a set of possible forces ($F_{\text{friction}} \in [-\mu F_n, \mu F_n]$). These idealizations need not satisfy Lipschitz continuity, the condition that small state changes produce proportionally bounded changes in the dynamics. Real compliance spreads contact over time, but offline averages can still hide the load and task consequences of crossing the contact boundary:

1. **Why action cosine similarity fails**: In representation learning and behavior modeling, action cosine similarity:
   $$\text{Cosine}(\hat{a}, a^*) = \frac{\hat{a}^\top a^*}{\|\hat{a}\| \|a^*\|}$$
   is widely used to measure directional alignment between predicted and expert commands. In physical contact, however, cosine similarity is dangerously deceptive because it completely discards command magnitude. Directional alignment without force calibration is useless: a policy proposal with 0.999 cosine similarity that commands 25 percent insufficient force stalls against the latch spring without overcoming static stiction ($F_t < \mu_s F_n$), stranding the robot indefinitely. Conversely, a proposal with 0.999 cosine similarity that commands 150 percent of the required force can overload the contact, potentially crossing the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire. Whether damage occurs depends on precontact energy, compliance, and the protective response; a trip is not evidence that the latch sheared.

2. **Why action mean squared error fails**: In offline supervised validation, Mean Squared Error:
   $$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^d (\hat{a}_j - a_j^*)^2$$
   weights every millimeter of position residual equally, regardless of physical context. In open-space transit, an end-effector tracking deviation of $2\text{ mm}$ is benign and easily recovered. For a separate hypothetical stiff-contact illustration, not the running warehouse latch, take local stiffness $k_{\text{contact}} \approx 5 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}$. Then an unmitigated $2\text{ mm}$ commanded penetration into the surface attempts to generate a normal reaction force:
   $$\Delta F = k_{\text{contact}} \Delta x = (5 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m})(0.002\,\text{m}) = 1{,}000\,\text{N}$$
   This illustrative stiffness calculation estimates the force associated with the commanded penetration, not a measured impact peak or a verified gearbox yield threshold. Actual compliance and protective response determine the realized load. Offline MSE gives that contact residual the same weight as a $2\text{ mm}$ drift in free space.

3. **Hardware instance variance at contact boundaries**: The sensitivity of contact dynamics exacerbates **hardware instance variance**. Unit-to-unit variations in joint backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$) and camera mounting tolerances ($\pm 1\text{ to }3\text{ mm}$) shift the spatial boundary of the contact interface. A policy trained on demonstrations logged on Unit 01 will encounter the physical latch surface earlier or later on Unit 02. Because contact is non-smooth, this microscopic spatial shift triggers immediate contact bifurcations: the arm either stalls in free space short of the latch or impacts the frame prematurely, causing physical jamming that offline evaluation on recorded logs can never expose.[^fn-math-contact-bifurcation]

The arm shows this exact disconnect in contact. An end-effector position error of a fraction of a millimeter per step scores as negligible Cartesian error offline, but on the latch that offset acts as a wedge. The latch's stiffness turns the lateral displacement into a reaction force ($F_{xy} = k_{\text{env}} \Delta_{xy}$) that climbs past the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire, which ends the attempt before the door unlatches.

[^fn-math-contact-bifurcation]: **Contact transitions in ideal models**\index{Contact mechanics!bifurcation}: An ideal rigid-body impact produces a velocity jump ($v^+ \ne v^-$), while ideal static friction permits a range of forces. Smooth-dynamics assumptions can fail at these transitions. Real compliance regularizes the transient but does not make replay reveal whether a shifted contact will stick, slip, or jam.

Offline scores can also mislead in the pessimistic direction when the task admits several valid actions. If the demonstrator passed an obstacle on the left, an open-loop score penalizes a candidate that passes on the right (the two-mode case of @sec-training-synthesis-regimes), although in closed loop both reach the goal. An action-level error measures divergence from one recording, not satisfaction of the task.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Open-loop prediction loss contrasts with the photon-to-actuation age-of-information bounds analyzed in @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
:::

::: {#fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open vs. closed loop divergence**: A persistent $1.0^\circ$ heading offset gives `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_math` angular mean squared error on recorded centerline states. On the mobile manipulator's aisle, the navigation stack's admitted motion with that fixed heading drifts linearly and reaches the `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_str` side clearance after `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str` at the `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit.
