Right: if that heading persists in a physical rollout at 1.5 meters per second, lateral drift grows linearly and reaches the 15-centimeter side clearance after about 5.7 seconds, 8.6 meters along the aisle. Policy proposals pass through the permission path before the plant moves."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPEN-LOOP REPLAY VS. CLOSED-LOOP DRIFT (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop
# │ Goal:    show why a heading error that is invisible offline spends clearance
# │ Show:    lateral offset against forward position, replay beside physical loop
# │ How:     one heading offset drives both panels and both numbers;
# │          speed and clearance come from the aisle via calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

COLORS = viz.COLORS

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario parameters) ────────────────────────────────────────────
HEADING_OFFSET_DEG = AisleDrift.heading_offset_deg  # category: illustrative; from the LEGO cell
CLEARANCE_M = AisleDrift.clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative; AISLE.side_clearance
SPEED_MS = AisleDrift.v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude  # category: illustrative; RM.base.max_velocity (drive limit)
REACH_M = 10.0  # category: chosen; plot extent, the first third of the aisle

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theta = math.radians(HEADING_OFFSET_DEG)
angular_mse = theta**2  # rad^2, the offline error signal
exhausted_m = CLEARANCE_M / math.tan(theta)  # where the drift reaches clearance
exhausted_s = exhausted_m / SPEED_MS

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, (ax_a, ax_b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), sharey=True)
x = np.linspace(0, REACH_M, 400)

ax_a.plot(x, np.zeros_like(x), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_a.plot(np.arange(0, REACH_M, 2), np.zeros(int(REACH_M // 2)), "o", ms=5, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])
ax_a.text(
    0.6,
    0.107,
    "Each next input returns to\nthe recorded centerline",
    fontsize=9,
    va="center",
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="white", ec=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.0),
)
ax_a.text(0.6, 0.030, f"Angular MSE: {angular_mse:.2e} rad$^2$".replace("e-04", r" $\times$ 10$^{-4}$"), fontsize=9, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])

ax_b.plot(x, x * math.tan(theta), color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_b.axhline(0.0, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax_b.axvline(exhausted_m, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 2)))
ax_b.plot([exhausted_m], [CLEARANCE_M], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["RedLine"], zorder=5)
ax_b.text(
    exhausted_m - 0.35, CLEARANCE_M - 0.075, f"Clearance exhausted\nat {exhausted_s:.1f} s", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha="right", va="top"
)
ax_b.text(0.6, 0.182, f"y = x tan({HEADING_OFFSET_DEG:.0f}°) under fixed heading", fontsize=9)

for ax, title, lx, lha in ((ax_a, "(a) Recorded-state replay", REACH_M - 0.15, "right"), (ax_b, "(b) Physical closed loop", 0.6, "left")):
    ax.axhline(CLEARANCE_M, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.2, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
    ax.text(lx, CLEARANCE_M + 0.006, f"{CLEARANCE_M * 100:.0f} cm clearance", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha=lha, va="bottom")
    ax.set_xlim(0, REACH_M)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 0.225)
    ax.set_xticks(range(0, int(REACH_M) + 1, 2))
    ax.set_xlabel("Forward position (m)")
    ax.text(0.0, 1.02, title, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

ax_a.set_yticks([0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20])
ax_a.set_ylabel("Lateral offset (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

A policy whose residual errors concentrate at latch contact can rank below a policy with larger errors in forgiving free space. The possible ranking inversion is:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\pi_A) < \mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\pi_B) \quad \text{yet} \quad \text{ACR}(\pi_A) \ll \text{ACR}(\pi_B)$$
The campaign must therefore compare goal completion and contact behavior, rather than selecting the winner from an average action score.

The same gap separates each offline metric commonly reported for a learned policy from the machine failure it hides, and @tbl-07-offline-closed-loop-disconnect pairs each with the closed-loop measure that exposes it, among them the time to intervention $T_{\text{TTI}}$, measured from the start of policy authority to the first permission-path override (the permission path refuses a proposal and applies its fallback) or operator takeover. Together with Autonomous Completion Rate, MTBI, and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), these closed-loop measures reveal what offline tensors hide.

| Offline metric                     | Open-loop assumption                                             | Why it breaks in closed loop                                                                       | Failure on the machine                                                 | Closed-loop measure                                                                                                |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Action mean squared error**      | Small residuals give small path deviations                       | A persistent bias integrates into drift and carries the machine off the demonstrated states        | The base spends its rack clearance (stop or strike)                    | Peak deviation from the reference path; time to intervention\index{Time-to-Intervention!metric} ($T_{\text{TTI}}$) |
| **Discrete action accuracy**       | Correct labels on logged states give identical execution         | Benign alternatives and boundary excursions cost the same; errors correlated in time are invisible | Command chatter and joint over-torque                                  | Peak jerk; adherence to actuator torque limits                                                                     |
| **Cosine similarity**              | Collinear proposals give stable paths                            | Magnitude is ignored, so under-actuation stalls against static friction and over-actuation slips   | The base stalls or slips its wheels; the arm stalls short of the latch | Slip ratio and damping (@sec-appendix-control-slip)                                                                |
| **Negative log-likelihood**        | Likelihood at the expert action captures the action distribution | Valid alternatives, such as passing an obstacle on the other side, are penalized                   | Valid policies rejected; demonstrator noise imitated as jitter         | Closed-loop task success over randomized starts                                                                    |
| **Reconstruction or Chamfer loss** | Accurate scene prediction gives safe plans                       | Background pixels outweigh thin obstacles and contact geometry                                     | Phantom braking; clipping a cable or a glass partition                 | Measured clearance; barrier-condition invariance                                                                   |

: **Offline metrics and the closed-loop failures they hide**: Each open-loop metric assumes the demonstrator's state distribution is unaffected by policy error; on the machine, biases integrate into drift, valid alternatives are penalized, and shifted states produce boundary violations. {#tbl-07-offline-closed-loop-disconnect tbl-colwidths="[18,20,24,18,20]"}

### The proposal boundary in two-processor architectures {#sec-evaluation-proposal-boundary}

The disconnect between tensor arithmetic and physical execution also spans the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. In the two-processor implementation, offline trace replay on the application processor measures only whether neural inference executes within its memory and compute budgets. In physical closed-loop execution, each candidate proposal crosses to the microcontroller that runs the permission path. When its qualified observations expose an inadmissible proposal, the permission path adjusts or refuses that proposal. It invokes a state-appropriate fallback when the active command can no longer continue under its own constraints and lease. Evaluating a policy offline, without the physical plant and the permission path in the loop, evaluates tensor arithmetic, not the survival of the machine; only the closed loop measures the path excursion, the intervention timing, and the permission path's measured performance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Deterministic gatekeeping and stopping envelopes for unverified neural policies are derived in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes.
:::

Open-loop scores cannot certify a closed loop, so the evidence about the proposer must come from executions whose conditions are known and recorded. Every setting in which a policy can be executed changes some part of the loop, whether the plant, the sensor stream, or the authority over the actuators, and @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes sorts those settings by what each can and cannot show.

## Evidence Regimes {#sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes}

Before its twenty door runs, the latch policy could have been scored against its logged demonstrations, run against a simulated door, run in shadow while a validated controller held the arm, or run on the real door with its contact tripwire armed. These four settings are the **evidence regimes**\index{Evidence regimes!definition} of @fig-07-evidence-regimes and @tbl-07-evidence-regimes, namely recorded replay, closed-loop simulation, shadow operation, and constrained physical testing. Each establishes a different relationship between the policy, its sensory inputs, and the state of the machine, so each supports a bounded claim. None of the four establishes how the unassisted policy behaves during unconstrained physical deployment, because each regime alters either the causal feedback of the control loop or the distribution of states the machine encounters.

### The four evaluation evidence regimes {#sec-evaluation-four-regimes}

The four testing settings differ fundamentally along two orthogonal dimensions: causal feedback coupling and environmental dynamics grounding. The first dimension, causal feedback, dictates whether the candidate policy's actions directly alter the physical states and sensory observations it will encounter on subsequent timesteps ($\partial s_{t+1}/\partial a_t \ne 0$), or whether the policy merely evaluates a pre-recorded, immutable stream of observations. In an open-loop setting, errors cannot compound across time, whereas in a closed-loop setting, control deviations can change later inputs and accumulate into trajectory drift; their growth rate depends on the dynamics and feedback. The second dimension, environmental dynamics grounding, determines whether sensory inputs originate from authentic physical transducers interacting with unmodeled contact mechanics, tire slip, and ambient entropy ($f_{\text{real}}$), or from idealized numerical simulations and recorded demonstration buffers ($f_{\text{sim}}$).

No single evaluation modality can maximize both axes simultaneously without exposing either high-value physical hardware or human bystanders to severe mechanical damage during early policy exploration. Consequently, empirical evaluation requires navigating a structured trade-off space across four distinct quadrants. As mapped in @fig-07-evidence-regimes, each evidence regime isolates specific computational or physical claims while accepting distinct, well-defined epistemic blind spots.

::: {#fig-07-evidence-regimes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Evaluation evidence regimes**: The regimes vary along causal feedback (open vs. closed loop) and physical realism (logged or synthetic vs. live hardware). Replay cannot observe compounding drift, simulation leaves the reality gap open, shadow operation locks the trajectory to the baseline controller, and constrained testing truncates failures at the constraint boundary $\partial\mathcal{S}$. No single regime tests deployment beyond that boundary." fig-alt="Evaluation evidence regimes decision manifold. A two-axis coordinate schematic mapping physical realism (vertical: synthetic and logged buffers to live hardware) against causal feedback (horizontal: open loop to closed loop). Four quadrants detail signal routing: Shadow Mode (top-left) feeds live sensor streams from the physical plant to both an active baseline controller driving motors and a candidate policy whose proposals are muted; Constrained Testing (top-right) closes the embodied control loop through a Control Barrier Function (CBF) veto gate on physical hardware bounded by a safety envelope ∂S; Recorded Replay (bottom-left) evaluates open-loop offline metric loss against static demonstration buffers without environment state updates; and Simulation (bottom-right) closes the causal loop using synthetic physics and raytraced observations subject to the reality gap."}
![](images/svg/fig07_evidence_regimes.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In recorded replay, the policy executes as a feedforward computation on stored sensor buffers. The environment does not respond to the policy outputs, and the state sequence remains fixed to the trajectory recorded during data collection. This regime supports claims about computational throughput, memory allocation, and loss against a logged dataset, such as whether inference fits its latency budget on the onboard accelerator and whether its numerical outputs match the recorded actions. It cannot support any claim about closed-loop stability, because the predicted action never alters the next observation; if the policy outputs a hard left turn, the next recorded frame still shows the base driving straight.

Closed-loop simulation restores the causal feedback loop by substituting an explicit mathematical model, $f_{\text{sim}}$, for the physical machine and its surroundings. When the policy proposes an action and the modeled permission path selects $u_t$, the simulation integrates the equations of motion, updates the scene, and renders synthetic sensor inputs for the next cycle at index $t+1$. This regime supports claims about the policy's behavior under the modeled dynamics, such as whether the base recovers from an initial offset or the arm avoids self-collision across its workspace, and thousands of instances can run in parallel. The evidence holds only for $f_{\text{sim}}$; unmodeled backlash\index{Mechanical backlash}, tire slip, contact friction\index{Contact friction} transitions, and lighting are excluded by construction, so stabilizing $f_{\text{sim}}$ says nothing yet about the hardware.

Shadow operation mounts the candidate policy onto an active physical machine while a validated baseline controller, or a human operator, retains authority over the actuators. The candidate policy receives live sensor frames, runs onboard inference under real mechanical vibration and bus traffic, and computes candidate actions $a_t^{\text{cand}}$.[^fn-hw-hil-bus] These candidate actions are logged but never dispatched to the motor drives. Shadow operation supports claims about execution timing, such as whether the latch policy holds its chosen `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str` chunk rate under operational thermal load, and about how often $a_t^{\text{cand}}$ diverges from the baseline action $a_t^{\text{base}}$ by more than a stated threshold. However, shadow mode suffers from the **trajectory confinement problem**: because the baseline controller retains sole authority over the actuators, the physical machine follows the trajectory distribution $d^{\pi_{\text{base}}}$ generated by the baseline. If the candidate policy proposes an action that would drift off the path, collide with a rack, or jam the latch, the physical plant never executes it. The candidate's sensory stream is perpetually confined to the baseline's state distribution, so the test campaign never observes whether the policy could have recovered from an unvisited state or whether its proposed motion would have caused hardware destruction.

[^fn-hw-hil-bus]: **Hardware-in-the-loop bus contention**\index{Hardware-in-the-loop!bus contention}: While neural accelerator inference latency may exhibit low variance in isolation, shared PCIe backplanes, direct memory access (DMA) transfers, and CAN bus arbitration introduce variable transport jitter under production workloads. A nominal inference cycle can stretch under memory bus saturation, depleting the phase margin of high-rate control loops. In shadow mode, this latency jitter is logged across real bus traffic without exposing the physical chassis to the resulting trajectory oscillations.

Constrained physical testing closes the causal loop on real hardware by letting candidate proposals reach the actuators within a bounded envelope. Boundaries take the form of physical tethers, velocity clamps, padded test cells, or the permission path itself (@sec-boundary-machine-model), which refuses unsafe commands at a validated response rate. This regime supports claims about contact dynamics, actuator saturation, and sensor noise within the tested envelope, which is why the twenty door runs belong to it.

An intervention changes or truncates the raw candidate's trajectory ($I_i \ge 1, A_i = 0$), leaving its unmitigated consequence unobserved. The permitted whole-machine trajectory may still complete the task. Constrained trials therefore report completion, intervention, and recovery metrics inside the tested envelope. Counting an intercepted run as an unassisted pass commits the **censored trial fallacy**, crediting the policy with protection supplied by the supervisor.

Some properties transfer across regime boundaries. Numerical outputs for identical input tensors transfer, as do algorithmic invariants, so an overflow that saturates an output in simulation saturates it on hardware given the same input; measured timing and memory pressure must be retested under each regime's bus, thermal, and scheduling load. The state distribution does not transfer. The moment the environment model changes from $f_{\text{sim}}$ to $f_{\text{real}}$, or the tested permission path changes, the sequence of states $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_t$ diverges.

Viewing these regimes as a ladder of fidelity is a trap. Advancing from replay to simulation to shadow mode to constrained testing does not strengthen one confidence claim; each step trades one distortion for another. Simulation buys closed-loop causality at the price of real sensing and contact, shadow mode trades causality back for real sensor streams and hardware timing, and constrained testing restores both but censors the states beyond its safety boundary. Zero interventions across a hundred constrained trials show that the trajectories stayed where the constraints never engaged, not that the failure rate outside the envelope is low. Each question belongs in the regime able to answer it (@tbl-07-evidence-regimes). For the latch policy, whether inference fits the chunk period belongs in replay and then in shadow operation on the target hardware; whether the arm recovers from a misplaced first contact belongs in simulation, where thousands of offsets cost no wear; and whether the door's spring and the gripper's compliance keep contact force below the limit belongs only in constrained physical trials. Each regime is blind to the failure modes of the others.

| Evaluation Evidence Regime       | Causal Feedback Coupling                              | Environmental Dynamics Grounding                         | Supported Empirical Evidence                            | Masked Failure Mode / Boundary Distortion                                            |
|:---------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Recorded Replay**              | Open Loop ($\partial s_{t+1}/\partial \hat{a}_t = 0$) | Static Demonstration Buffers $\mathcal{D}_{\text{demo}}$ | Latency budget, DRAM footprint, numerical accuracy      | Covariate shift; errors never alter subsequent observations                          |
| **Closed-Loop Simulation**       | Closed Loop ($s_{t+1} = f_{\text{sim}}(s_t, u_t)$)    | Synthetic Physics Operator $f_{\text{sim}}$              | Kinematic reachability, large parallel test suites      | Sim-to-real gap; unmodeled contact non-linearities and tire slip                     |
| **Shadow Mode Operation**        | Open Loop for candidate (actions muted)               | Physical machine $f_{\text{real}}$                       | Bus contention, thermal throttling, real sensor noise   | Trajectory confinement; states locked to baseline controller $d^{\pi_{\text{base}}}$ |
| **Constrained Physical Testing** | Closed Loop with runtime veto ($u_{\text{safe}}$)     | Physical machine $f_{\text{real}}$ within envelope       | Contact dynamics, compliance, friction, actuator limits | State censorship; permission-path overrides and tethers truncate failure tails       |

: **Evaluation evidence regimes compared**: Trade-offs between causal feedback coupling, environmental realism, supported empirical claims, and experimental boundary distortions across the four testing regimes. No single environment evaluates open deployment; rigorous certification requires combining complementary regimes rather than assuming a linear fidelity ladder. {#tbl-07-evidence-regimes tbl-colwidths="[20,20,20,20,20]"}

### Simulation as a conditional proxy {#sec-evaluation-proxy-transfer-law}

A simulator can screen latch candidates before scarce physical trials, but its usefulness depends on agreement for the mechanisms the decision uses. The paired probes in @sec-training compare contact and timing channel by channel. Evaluation carries those discrepancies into its test plan: a favorable simulated recovery nominates a physical trial; it does not close the manifest's contact or transport omissions. Visual rendering, friction regularization, and missing force observations can each change candidate rankings.

### System identification vs. domain randomization {#sec-evaluation-sysid-domain-randomization}

The training methods of @sec-training leave an evaluation obligation: identify which physical variations the simulator represents and which remain absent. Calibration and randomization matter here because they determine what a simulated trial can support. Their evaluation role is to expose the limits of the proxy before its scores influence the physical campaign.

A physics engine represents link masses, inertias, motor constants, friction, and damping through a parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \Xi$. Calibration and randomization address different uncertainties in the parameterized operator $f_{\text{sim}}(\cdot; \boldsymbol{\xi})$ relative to the physical plant $f_{\text{real}}$:

**System Identification (SysID)**:
SysID treats the physics parameters $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ as unknown deterministic constants to be calibrated against physical telemetry. Given a calibration dataset of logged hardware trajectories $\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}} = \{(s_t^{\text{real}}, u_t^{\text{real}}, s_{t+1}^{\text{real}})\}_{t=1}^K$, SysID solves a non-linear parameter optimization problem:
$$\boldsymbol{\xi}^* = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \Xi} \sum_{t=1}^K \left\| s_{t+1}^{\text{real}} - f_{\text{sim}}(s_t^{\text{real}}, u_t^{\text{real}}; \boldsymbol{\xi}) \right\|_2^2$$
A calibration vector $\boldsymbol{\xi}^*_{\text{Unit 01}}$ characterizes the unit and conditions that supplied its telemetry. Hardware differences, heating, and wear can move the plant away from that estimate, so evaluation needs held-out trajectories and units. Parameter fitting also cannot recover a mechanism absent from the simulator's equations, such as unmodeled backlash or wiring harness drag.

**Domain Randomization (DR)**:
Rather than seeking a single point estimate $\boldsymbol{\xi}^*$, Domain Randomization treats the physical parameters as random variables sampled from an epistemic prior distribution $p(\boldsymbol{\Xi})$ during closed-loop policy training:
$$\theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\xi} \sim p(\boldsymbol{\Xi})} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t R(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t)) \right], \quad \text{subject to } s_{t+1} = f_{\text{sim}}(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t); \boldsymbol{\xi})$$
By exposing the candidate policy to randomized variations in surface friction ($\mu \sim \mathcal{U}[0.3, 1.2]$), link masses, and disturbance impulses across millions of parallel simulated rollouts, DR optimizes expected return over the chosen parameter distribution. It does not certify stability at every point in its support.

However, DR is vulnerable to the **conservatism trap**: if the randomization distribution $p(\boldsymbol{\Xi})$ is chosen excessively wide (for instance, forcing a single manipulation policy to remain stable simultaneously across frictionless ice and high-friction rubber), the expected-return objective may spend capacity on conditions irrelevant to the intended deployment. It does not become a worst-case objective merely because the support is wide. On real hardware, this manifests as high-frequency torque chatter, sluggish motion, or an inability to generate sufficient contact force to overcome nominal static friction. Conversely, if $p(\boldsymbol{\Xi})$ is chosen too narrow, the policy collapses the moment physical hardware encounters unmodeled environmental conditions.

### Hardware-in-the-loop simulation and transport fidelity {#sec-evaluation-hil-simulation}

Even a simulation operator calibrated via SysID and broadened by Domain Randomization remains vulnerable to execution distortions if evaluated purely in software. In **Software-in-the-Loop (SIL)** simulation, both neural policy inference and physics integration execute as software processes on a host workstation or cloud compute cluster. SIL evaluates algorithmic convergence and gross kinematics across massive parallel rollout batches, but it advances in synthetic virtual time $\Delta t$. In this idealized virtual environment, the physics solver pauses while neural inference computes, completely abstracting away physical compute latencies, direct memory access (DMA) overhead, and operating system scheduling jitter.

On an embodied physical machine, real time marches forward continuously on the hardware crystal clock. The true physical **end-to-end transport and inference latency** spans the entire perception-to-actuation pipeline:
$$t_{\text{e2e}} = t_{\text{sensor}} + t_{\text{dma}} + t_{\text{infer}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{actuator}}$$
In a closed feedback loop, transport delay $t_{\text{e2e}}$ means commands are applied to yesterday's state. Delay adds phase lag to the feedback loop. If it exhausts the stability margin, a correction intended to damp motion can reinforce an oscillation instead. Increased $t_{\text{e2e}}$ from bus contention, dropped frames, or thermal throttling can therefore amplify tracking errors. Whether instability develops depends on the controller and plant; the campaign must also test whether the independent permission path refuses stale motion and executes its fallback in time.

**Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL)** simulation closes this execution gap by mounting the compiled policy binary and the deterministic permission path directly onto target edge silicon (the application processor and safety microcontroller), connected across physical communication buses (PCIe, CAN, or SerDes). While a dedicated real-time digital simulator synthesizes the physical plant and streams rendered sensor frames over hardware interfaces (such as FPD-Link or GMSL deserializers) at line rate, the edge processor executes inference under real clock deadlines, shared memory contention, and thermal throttling.

HIL audits the proposal boundary under real hardware constraints. The campaign separately timestamps capture, dispatch, admission, active-lease expiry, and physical response; evidence keeps aging throughout. The running machine's `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` active chunk lease is not an allowance for the entire sensing-to-actuation path. A late replacement is refused, while an already admitted output may continue only while its own state, evidence, and lease remain valid. Loss of those premises invokes the validated fallback. A simulator that pauses virtual time during inference cannot expose this deadline behavior without an explicit delay model.

Consequently, while closed-loop simulation (spanning SIL and HIL) serves as an effective screening filter for policy candidates, physical trial limits remain the ultimate arbiter of embodied competence.

::: {#chk-eval-evidence-regimes .callout-checkpoint title="Trade-offs across evidence regimes"}

Before evaluating physical trial limits, verify your understanding of evidence regimes and fidelity trade-offs:

- [ ] **Regime causality trade-offs**: Can you contrast the causal feedback properties of recorded trace replay against closed-loop simulation?
- [ ] **Shadow-mode trajectory confinement**: Can you explain why shadow-mode evaluation on the running machine cannot test the candidate policy's recovery maneuvers?
- [ ] **Transfer across regimes**: Can you describe which properties transfer reliably across regimes and which one stays behind?

:::

## Fixing the Trial Protocol {#sec-evaluation-trial-protocol}

Because success probability and intervention rates are defined only with respect to a specific joint distribution $\mathcal{D}$, the intended operating region must be declared before trials are sampled. The **target Operational Design Domain (ODD)**\index{Operational design domain!target ODD} is the part of the declared ODD (@sec-training-policy-manifest) that the evaluation samples; its sampling weights define $\mathcal{D}$, and no evaluation claim reaches beyond it. If an engineering team executes fifty physical runs across ad hoc trajectories and reports a 90 percent pass rate, the denominator corresponds to an undefined population. A measured success rate supports a target-distribution claim only when the support and sampling weights of $\mathcal{D}$ are specified in advance, establishing explicit bounds on illuminance, payload ranges, surface friction coefficients, allowable initial state offsets, and the specific hardware serial numbers tested.

Extracting valid confidence bounds from empirical trials requires three operational conditions:

1. *Independent and Identically Distributed (i.i.d.) Sampling:* Trials must be independent realizations drawn from $\mathcal{D}$. Shuffling a validation split does not by itself make correlated source observations independent. On physical hardware, thermal accumulation in motor windings ($I^2 R$), battery voltage sag, and progressive mechanical backlash create temporal autocorrelation across trials. Run 20 is fundamentally not drawn from the same physical distribution as Run 1 unless adequate thermal cooldown and battery recharging intervals are strictly enforced. Furthermore, trials executed on a single hardware unit (Unit 01) cannot be treated as i.i.d. draws from the fleet distribution $\mathcal{M}$.
2. *Fixed Outcome Predicates:* The binary evaluation function $\phi$ and the termination criteria $\kappa$ must remain fixed throughout the campaign. Modifying the time horizon $T_{\max}$ or adjusting the spatial tolerance of the goal region $g$ midway through testing alters the definition of success, committing post-hoc metric drift.
3. *Full-Denominator Accounting:* Every initiated run remains in the ledger, including hardware aborts, timeouts, protective stops, and human takeovers. An abort that prevents goal completion has $Y = 0$; any counted override gives $A = 0$ under the strict autonomy metric. A normal adjustment followed by on-time completion may have $Y = 1$ and $A = 0$. Protection outcomes record limit crossings and damage separately. Interception leaves the unmitigated trajectory unknown, so zero damage cannot be credited as evidence of unassisted survival. Dropping any of these runs changes the denominator and the question being answered.

When these conditions hold, the sample mean estimates the declared closed-loop outcome under $\mathcal{D}$. The remaining question is how much uncertainty a finite sample leaves, even when every recorded outcome is a success.

## Confidence from a Finite Campaign {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-clopper-pearson-zero-failure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOPPER-PEARSON ZERO-FAILURE RELIABILITY SIZING (LEGO)

# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the takeaways.
# │ Show: One-sided confidence limits for iid zero-failure trials, not a rate estimate.
# │ How: p_lower = alpha^(1/n); failure_upper = 1 - p_lower.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt, check, MarkdownStr

class ClopperPearsonZeroFailure:
    """Exact binomial confidence bounds for physical robotics qualification."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_runs = 20  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign's clean runs
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    alpha = 1.0 - confidence  # category: derived; significance level
    n_one_in = 8  # category: illustrative; a policy that fails one run in eight
    n_fallacy = 1000  # category: illustrative; clean openings in the perfect-record fallacy
    n_looks = 5  # category: illustrative; independent 5 percent looks in the optional-stopping example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_lower = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_runs, confidence=confidence)
    failure_upper = 1.0 - p_lower
    p_clean_one_in = (1.0 - 1.0 / n_one_in) ** n_runs  # chance that policy still logs n_runs clean runs

    # Scaling to 99.9% reliability
    p_target_999 = 0.999
    n_req_999 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_999, confidence=confidence)
    p_lower_fallacy = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_fallacy, confidence=confidence)
    p_any_false_positive = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) ** n_looks  # chance of at least one false positive across independent looks

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(p_lower - 0.8609) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run lower bound")
    check(abs(failure_upper - 0.1391) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run upper confidence limit")
    check(n_req_999 == 2995, "Unexpected sample size for 99.9% reliability")
    check(n_one_in == 8 and abs(p_clean_one_in - 0.0692) < 0.001, "Unexpected clean-record probability for a one-in-eight policy")
    check(p_lower_fallacy < p_target_999 and abs(p_lower_fallacy - 0.9970) < 0.0001, "The 1,000-run bound must fall short of 99.9 percent")
    check(abs(p_any_false_positive - 0.2262) < 0.001, "Five independent 5 percent looks should give about 22.6 percent")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_runs_str = fmt_int(n_runs)
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0)
    p_lower_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lower, precision=1)
    failure_upper_pct_str = fmt_percent(failure_upper, precision=1)
    p_lower_val_str = fmt(p_lower, precision=3)
    n_req_999_str = fmt_int(n_req_999, commas=True)
    _words = {5: "five", 8: "eight"}
    n_one_in_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_one_in])
    p_clean_one_in_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_clean_one_in, precision=1)
    n_fallacy_str = fmt_int(n_fallacy, commas=True)
    p_lower_fallacy_str = fmt(p_lower_fallacy, precision=4)
    n_looks_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_looks].capitalize())
    p_any_false_positive_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_any_false_positive, precision=1)
```

With the outcome, population, regime, and denominator fixed, the twenty clean nominal runs leave a statistical question. A confidence bound states how much uncertainty remains under the declared sampling model; it does not estimate failure severity or authorize deployment.

A normal-approximation Wald interval collapses at an observed success fraction of one because its estimated variance vanishes. That collapse reflects a failed approximation, not certainty. For the predeclared zero-failure campaign, the exact one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bound\index{Clopper-Pearson non-asymptotic bound!definition}\index{Clopper-Pearson method} [@clopper1934use] follows by asking which success probability would produce all $n$ successes with probability $\alpha$:
$$p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}$$
and the corresponding exact upper bound on failure probability:
$$p_{\text{fail, upper}} = 1 - \alpha^{1/n}$$
The related zero-event exposure derivations are collected in @sec-appendix-ml-exposure; campaigns with failures require the general binomial inversion. Here the zero-failure result is enough to decide what the nominal door record supports.

For rare failure rates ($p_{\text{fail}} \ll 1$), we obtain the celebrated **Rule of Three**\index{Rule of Three} [@hanley1983nothing] via first-order Taylor expansion: $\ln(1 - p_{\text{fail}}) = -p_{\text{fail}} - \frac{p_{\text{fail}}^2}{2} - \dots \approx -p_{\text{fail}}$. Setting the zero-failure probability $(1 - p_{\text{fail}})^n = \alpha = 0.05$ implies $n \ln(1 - p_{\text{fail}}) = \ln(0.05) \approx -2.9957 \approx -3.0$. Substituting the linear expansion yields $-n p_{\text{fail}} \approx -3.0$, establishing that when $n$ independent trials pass with zero failures, the upper 95 percent confidence bound on failure probability is approximately:
$$p_{\text{fail, upper}}^{95\%} \approx \frac{3}{n}.$$ {#eq-eval-rule-of-three}
For the twenty door runs, @eq-eval-rule-of-three yields $p_{\text{fail, upper}}^{95\%} \approx 3/20 = 0.15$. The exact computation in \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} tightens this to a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent failure upper limit, which leaves the machine far short of 95 percent demonstrated reliability. Crucially, this non-asymptotic formulation demonstrates why **twenty trials cannot prove 99 percent reliability**. To mathematically certify a 99 percent operational reliability lower bound ($p_{\text{target}} = 0.99$, or $p_{\text{fail}} = 0.01$) at 95 percent confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$), the required zero-failure sample size inverts to:
$$n = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(\alpha)}{\ln(p_{\text{target}})} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.99)} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{-2.99573}{-0.01005} \right\rceil = 299 \text{ consecutive trials}$$
By contrast, twenty consecutive failure-free runs certify a lower bound of merely $p_{\text{lower}} = (0.05)^{1/20} \approx 0.8609$ (86.1 percent), leaving a massive 13.9 percent probability of physical failure unrefuted. Believing that twenty clean runs demonstrate a 99 percent reliable machine is an error of almost fifteen-fold in statistical exposure ($299$ versus $20$). A defective policy that fails once in every `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_one_in_str` runs ($p = 0.875$) still completes twenty consecutive runs cleanly `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` percent of the time—so a clean observed fraction alone cannot qualify that checkpoint at a higher reliability target.[^fn-math-rule-three]

Moreover, this statistical bound assumes stationary, identically distributed draws across trials—an assumption routinely shattered on physical testbeds by **hardware instance variance**. If twenty trials are executed on a single physical robot (Unit 01), they characterize that unit's individual harmonic drive gear backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 1\text{ mrad}$), motor torque constant tolerance ($\pm 5$ percent), and sensor mounting alignment. When deployed onto Unit 02, differing machining tolerances, gear backlash, and structural compliance alter the physical transfer function, converting nominal runs into latch jams without changing a single neural weight.

[^fn-math-rule-three]: **Continuous-time Poisson equivalence of the Rule of Three**: The Rule of Three applies equally to continuous-time Poisson processes with constant hazard rate $\lambda$. If an autonomous machine operates for total failure-free duration $T$ without an intervention, the probability of zero Poisson arrivals is $P(N(T) = 0) = e^{-\lambda T}$. Equating this to significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ yields $-\lambda T = \ln(0.05) \approx -2.9957$, proving that the 95 percent upper confidence limit on failure rate is $\lambda_{\text{upper}} \approx 3.0/T$, or conversely that bounding $\lambda \le \lambda_{\text{target}}$ requires exposure time $T \ge 3.0 / \lambda_{\text{target}}$. To certify a target Mean Time Between Failures of $\text{MTBF} = 1/\lambda_{\text{target}}$, an autonomous system must execute uninterrupted physical testing for at least three times the target MTBF ($T \ge 3.0 \times \text{MTBF}$) without a single failure or intervention.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_nonasymptotic_reliability_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing trial sample sizes against achievable statistical reliability bounds."}
*Twenty consecutive zero-failure runs bound reliability at only 86 percent, requiring thousands of runs for high-assurance certification.*
:::

::: {#nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound .callout-notebook title="Derivation of the 20-run lower bound"}
**Problem**: The mobile manipulator completes $n =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` physical door-opening runs with zero contact-tripwire crossings or human interventions ($k =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str`). What is the exact one-sided `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.confidence_pct_str` percent lower confidence bound on its true operational success probability $p$?

**Mathematical Derivation**: For independent, identically distributed Bernoulli trials from the declared operational test distribution, $p_{\text{lower}}$ is the success probability at which `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` consecutive successes have probability $\alpha=0.05$. Thus the one-sided 95 percent lower confidence limit is $p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n} = (0.05)^{1/20} \approx$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent); the corresponding failure-probability upper confidence limit is `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent.

**Systems insight**: The observation "`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` out of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` passed" supplies a confidence limit under those sampling assumptions, not an observed failure rate, a mean interval between failures, or a deployment permission. Inverting the bound gives the trials a target needs, $n = \lceil \ln\alpha / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$\index{Clopper-Pearson method!sample size bound}, so a $99.9$ percent success lower limit requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` consecutive zero-failure trials drawn from the target distribution.
:::

The nominal door result now has a defined interpretation. Raising the desired lower limit changes the trial count and the physical cost of collecting it.

## Physical Trial Limits {#sec-evaluation-trial-limits}

A reliability claim is paid for in trials. The core dilemma of physical AI evaluation is the irreconcilable collision between statistical sample-size scaling and physical hardware fatigue. In software testing, executing a million unit tests consumes only processor clock cycles; in embodied systems, executing trials consumes wall-clock time, generates mechanical bearing wear, fatigues structural linkages, and heats motor windings. Choosing an evaluation regime settles what a test can show, but on a physical machine the plant, not the compute budget, fixes what each closed-loop trial costs, and statistics fixes how many trials the claim demands. Sizing a qualification campaign requires balancing the statistical power needed to bound rare catastrophic failures against the finite fatigue life of the physical testbed. Those two quantities together separate a qualification argument from an anecdote.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-cycle
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WALL-CLOCK COST OF THE DOOR CAMPAIGN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-trial-limits, @nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance,
# │          @fig-07-confidence-bounds, and @tbl-07-confidence-bounds.
# │ Show: one door trial's test-cell time (run plus reset) and what the
# │       opening campaign and a 99.9 percent campaign occupy at that cycle.
# │ How: T_cycle = t_run + t_reset; T_campaign = n * T_cycle, with n from
# │      calc_zero_failure_sample_size.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time, fmt_int, check, MarkdownStr

class DoorCycle:
    """Test-cell time per door trial and per zero-failure campaign."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_run = 25.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; drive-in from the standoff, stop, guarded unlatch and swing
    t_reset = 15.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; re-latch, return to the standoff, telemetry flush
    n_opening = 20  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign's clean runs
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    p_target = 0.999  # category: chosen; success lower limit the section argues toward
    n_operators = 2  # category: illustrative; safety operators watching each run
    table_n = (10, 20, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2995)  # category: chosen; rows of @tbl-07-confidence-bounds

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_cycle = (t_run + t_reset).to(ureg.second)
    n_target = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target, confidence=confidence)
    t_opening = (n_opening * t_cycle).to(minute)
    t_target = (n_target * t_cycle).to(ureg.hour)
    t_target_days = t_target.to(ureg.day)
    t_target_operator = t_target * n_operators
    shifts_target = (t_target_operator / (8.0 * ureg.hour)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    table_hours = [n * c for n, c in zip(table_n, [t_cycle.to(ureg.hour)] * len(table_n))]  # zip: class scope is not visible inside the comprehension

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_cycle.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Door cycle should be 40 s")
    check(n_target == 2995, "Zero-failure trials for a 99.9 percent lower limit should be 2,995")
    check(abs(t_opening.to(minute).magnitude - 13.33) < 0.005, "Twenty runs should take about 13.3 min")
    check(abs(t_target.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 33.28) < 0.005, "2,995 runs should take about 33.3 h")
    check(abs(t_target_operator.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 66.56) < 0.01, "Two operators should spend about 66.6 h")
    check(8 < shifts_target < 9, "Prose says over eight eight-hour shifts")
    check(table_n[-1] == n_target, "Last table row must be the 99.9 percent sample size")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_run_str = fmt_time(t_run, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_reset_str = fmt_time(t_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_cycle_str = fmt_time(t_cycle, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_opening_str = fmt_time(t_opening, unit=minute, precision=1)
    t_target_str = fmt_time(t_target, unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    t_target_days_str = fmt_time(t_target_days, unit=ureg.day, precision=1, style="word")
    t_target_operator_str = fmt_time(t_target_operator, unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    shifts_floor_str = MarkdownStr({8: "eight", 9: "nine"}[int(shifts_target)])
    n_operators_str = MarkdownStr({2: "two", 3: "three"}[n_operators])
    h_10_str = fmt_time(table_hours[0], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_20_str = fmt_time(table_hours[1], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_50_str = fmt_time(table_hours[2], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_100_str = fmt_time(table_hours[3], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_250_str = fmt_time(table_hours[4], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_500_str = fmt_time(table_hours[5], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_1000_str = fmt_time(table_hours[6], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_2995_str = fmt_time(table_hours[7], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
```

### Physical experimentation costs and hardware fatigue budgeting {#sec-evaluation-trial-costs}

A physical trial consumes more than the simulated step or log-replay time. It consumes wall-clock time, stresses mechanical linkages, heats motor windings, and risks physical damage to the hardware. The door campaign shows how the cost accumulates. In one run the base drives in from its `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` standoff and stops, and the arm then unlatches at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach and swings the door open, which together occupy `{python} DoorCycle.t_run_str` of the test cell (illustrative). The reset intended to support the next independent draw re-latches the door, returns the base to its standoff, and flushes the run's telemetry, adding `{python} DoorCycle.t_reset_str` (illustrative), so each trial costs `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str`.[^fn-math-trial-cost] At that cycle the twenty clean runs that opened the chapter took `{python} DoorCycle.t_opening_str`, and the campaign that a 99.9 percent success lower limit requires (\ref{nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance}) runs far longer, even before the arm's windings take any thermal rest (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles).

[^fn-math-trial-cost]: **Physical trial cycle budget**\index{Trial budget!wall-clock cost}: The duration of a physical trial includes the reset as well as the run, $T_{\text{trial}} = t_{\text{run}} + t_{\text{reset}} =$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_run_str` $+$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_reset_str` $=$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` for the door. Budgeting by active run time alone produces unrealistic testing timelines and tempts teams to truncate reset and cooldown intervals, which causes thermal non-stationarity across runs.

The plant also changes while the trials accumulate. The confidence bound assumes independent draws from a stationary process, and wear breaks stationarity: gearhead backlash, wheel radius, tire friction, and joint damping drift at rates that must be measured on the test hardware. Pooling a thousand runs then treats a progression of degrading machines as repeated tests of one, and a late failure may reflect the worn plant rather than the policy.

### Sample size requirements per empirical claim {#sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim}

The target success probability and confidence level determine the required evidence. If the facility cannot afford the corresponding exposure, the campaign must narrow its claim rather than report an underpowered result as qualification.

A zero-failure empirical campaign is sized by inverting the exact Clopper--Pearson binomial survival bound of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival for the trial count $n$:
$$n \ge \frac{\ln(1 - C)}{\ln(p_{\text{target}})}$$
where $C$ is the required statistical confidence (typically 95 percent, so $\alpha = 1 - C = 0.05$) and $p_{\text{target}}$ is the lower success probability threshold. For rare failure probabilities ($p_{\text{fail}} = 1 - p_{\text{target}} \ll 1$) at 95 percent confidence ($\ln(1 - C) = \ln(0.05) \approx -2.9957 \approx -3.0$), the first-order Taylor approximation $\ln(p_{\text{target}}) = \ln(1 - p_{\text{fail}}) \approx -p_{\text{fail}}$ connects this exact formula directly to the Rule of Three:
$$n \approx \frac{3}{p_{\text{fail}}} = \frac{3}{1 - p_{\text{target}}}.$$

The notebook below translates the target into a trial budget. A campaign with any failures needs the general binomial bound; it cannot recover a zero-failure claim by appending enough clean runs after inspecting the result.

Thus, the physical claim, not the test facility's schedule, fixes how many consecutive runs the robot must survive without a single failure (@fig-07-confidence-bounds and @tbl-07-confidence-bounds; derivations in @sec-appendix-ml-exposure). Notebook \ref{nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance} applies this formulation to calculate the real-world facility time and operator shifts demanded to certify high-reliability manipulation on the latch cell.

A fixed-sample zero-failure protocol may reject a candidate at the first failure; it never requires continued exposure to a dangerous policy. Early acceptance is a different decision. Stopping when the accumulating result looks favorable changes the test's error properties unless the stopping rule was calibrated in advance. @Sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt develops a sequential rule for both acceptance and rejection.

::: {#nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance .callout-notebook title="Statistical scaling of assurance"}
**Problem**: Suppose an evaluation target calls for a one-sided success lower limit of $p_{\text{target}} = 0.999$ at 95 percent confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$). If each door trial requires $T_{\text{trial}} =$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str`, how many zero-failure runs and how much wall-clock testing time are required?

**Calculations**: The inversion of \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} gives $n = \lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.999)\rceil = 2{,}995$ consecutive zero-failure trials. At `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` per trial, this demands $T_{\text{total}} =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` $\times$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` $\approx$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` (`{python} DoorCycle.t_target_days_str`) of continuous testing. With a `{python} DoorCycle.n_operators_str`-operator safety protocol, this consumes `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_operator_str` of operator time, or over `{python} DoorCycle.shifts_floor_str` eight-hour shifts.

**Systems insight**: Even on a cycle as short as the door's, a 99.9 percent lower limit costs `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_days_str` of continuous test-cell occupancy, and a longer cycle scales it in proportion. A component replacement during the campaign may require a new population definition rather than pooling incompatible runs.
:::

<!-- fig-alt below hand-types the door-cycle values because fig-alt cannot hold inline python. Keep them in sync:
     "33.3 hours" = DoorCycle.t_target_str; "40 seconds" = DoorCycle.t_cycle_str (guards in calc-evaluation-door-cycle). -->

::: {#fig-07-confidence-bounds fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Confidence bounds and testing budgets**: One-sided Clopper-Pearson success lower limits after zero failures at 90, 95, and 99 percent confidence. At 95 percent, `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` iid runs give `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent; 99.9 percent needs `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` runs, or `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` at the `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` door cycle." fig-alt="Success lower confidence limits rise with zero-failure trial count. The 95 percent curve is 86.1 percent at 20 trials and 99.9 percent at 2,995 trials; its complementary failure upper limits are 13.9 and 0.1 percent. The 2,995-trial annotation converts to 33.3 hours at 40 seconds per door run."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOPPER-PEARSON SUCCESS LOWER LIMITS AFTER ZERO FAILURES (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-confidence-bounds
# │ Goal:    show what a clean run of n physical trials can and cannot certify
# │ Show:    the lower limit against trial count, at three confidence levels
# │ How:     p_lower = (1 - c)**(1/n); every annotated value is derived here
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.2))

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario parameters) ────────────────────────────────────────────
CONFIDENCES = (0.90, 0.95, 0.99)  # category: chosen; plotted confidence levels
TARGET = 0.999  # category: chosen; the success lower limit the chapter argues toward
CYCLE_SECONDS = DoorCycle.t_cycle.to(ureg.second).magnitude  # category: illustrative; door cycle from calc-evaluation-door-cycle
REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE = 0.95  # category: chosen; the level both annotations read off

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def lower_limit(n, confidence):
    """One-sided Clopper-Pearson lower limit on success given zero failures."""
    return 100.0 * (1.0 - confidence) ** (1.0 / n)

n = np.logspace(1, np.log10(4200), 600)
small_n = 20
big_n = int(np.ceil(np.log(1.0 - REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE) / np.log(TARGET)))

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Ordered categories, not resources: one hue, distinguished by dash pattern.
for confidence, dash in zip(CONFIDENCES, [(0, (1, 2)), (0, ()), (0, (6, 3))]):
    ax.plot(n, lower_limit(n, confidence), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.0, linestyle=dash, label=f"{confidence:.0%} success lower limit")

ax.axhline(100.0 * TARGET, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax.text(10.6, 99.1, f"{100 * TARGET:.1f}% statistical target", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], va="top")

box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.0)
arrow = dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=4)
for n_pt, xy_text in ((small_n, (46, 76.5)), (big_n, (330, 93.2))):
    y_pt = lower_limit(n_pt, REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE)
    ax.plot([n_pt], [y_pt], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], zorder=5)
    if n_pt == small_n:
        label = f"{n_pt:,} trials\n{y_pt:.1f}% success lower\n" f"{100 - y_pt:.1f}% failure upper"
    else:
        label = f"{n_pt:,} trials\n{y_pt:.1f}% success lower\n" f"{n_pt * CYCLE_SECONDS / 3600:.1f} h at {CYCLE_SECONDS:.0f} s/run"
    ax.annotate(label, xy=(n_pt, y_pt), xytext=xy_text, textcoords="data", fontsize=8.5, bbox=box, arrowprops=arrow, va="center", ha="left")

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(10, 4200)
ax.set_ylim(60, 100.4)
ax.set_yticks(range(60, 101, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("Zero-failure trial count n (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Success lower confidence limit (%)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

@Fig-07-confidence-bounds maps this statistical reality across trial counts from 10 to 4,200 on a logarithmic horizontal axis against the success lower limit (60 to 100 percent) on the vertical axis:

- **Steep initial gains**: At small sample sizes, each additional clean trial produces substantial statistical leverage. For instance, twenty zero-failure trials (the left marked point) establish an $86.1$ percent success lower bound at 95 percent confidence (with an upper failure bound of $13.9$ percent).
- **Asymptotic flattening**: As the target reliability approaches unity, the curves flatten dramatically due to the logarithmic relationship $n = \lceil \ln(1-C) / \ln(p_{\text{target}}) \rceil$. Reaching a $99.9$ percent success lower limit at 95 percent confidence (the right marked point) demands $2{,}995$ consecutive zero-failure trials—requiring $33.3$ hours of continuous test-cell occupancy for a 40-second door cycle.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-confidence-table
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ZERO-FAILURE CONFIDENCE LIMITS FOR THE BOUNDS TABLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-07-confidence-bounds (statistics columns).
# │ Show: one-sided success lower limits at 90, 95, and 99 percent confidence
# │       and the 95 percent failure upper limit for each table row.
# │ How: p_lower = (1 - C)^(1/n) via calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound;
# │      rows are DoorCycle.table_n so the time column and these stay aligned.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, check

class ConfidenceBoundsTable:
    """Clopper-Pearson zero-failure limits for every row of the bounds table."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    table_n = DoorCycle.table_n  # category: chosen; rows of @tbl-07-confidence-bounds

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    lo90 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.90) for n in table_n]
    lo95 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.95) for n in table_n]
    lo99 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.99) for n in table_n]
    up95 = [1.0 - p for p in lo95]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(lo95[1] - ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower) < 1e-12, "20-run row must match the opening campaign's bound")
    check(abs(lo95[-1] - 0.999) < 1e-4, "Last row must meet the 99.9 percent target")
    check(all(a < b < c for a, b, c in zip(lo99, lo95, lo90)), "Higher confidence must give a lower success limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    lo90_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo90]
    lo95_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo95]
    lo99_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo99]
    up95_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in up95]
```
