:::

The constructed series in @fig-07-av-miles-scaling compare two kinds of exposure arithmetic. Their simulated-mile total cannot satisfy a physical-mile threshold, and neither series is an audited fleet history. The horizontal thresholds express the cited sampling assumptions, not standards compliance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-mtbf-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MTBF EXPOSURE CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the MTBF worked example after @fig-07-av-miles-scaling and
# │          @chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf.
# │ Show: exposure hours, zero-failure missions, calendar time, and wheel
# │       revolutions a single machine needs to bound a 1e-4 per hour rate.
# │ How: T = -ln(alpha) / lambda via calc_empirical_testing_exposure;
# │      N = ln(alpha) / ln(1 - lambda t_mission); N_rev = N v t / (pi D).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_math, sci_latex, fmt, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MtbfCampaign:
    """Zero-failure mission campaign that bounds a 1e-4 per hour rate on one machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    rate = 1e-4 / ureg.hour  # category: chosen; teaching target (MTBF 10,000 h)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    t_mission = 360.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; one retrieval mission
    t_reset = 120.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; dock recharge and telemetry reset
    d_wheel = 0.20 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; drive-wheel diameter
    l10_rev = 5.0e7  # category: illustrative; gearhead L10 rating, revolutions

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 1 - confidence
    t_cycle = t_mission + t_reset
    d_mission = (v * t_mission).to(ureg.meter)
    t_continuous = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(rate, confidence=confidence).to(ureg.hour)
    p_fail_mission = (rate * t_mission).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    n_req = math.log(alpha) / math.log(1 - p_fail_mission)
    t_calendar = (n_req * t_cycle).to(ureg.hour)
    n_rev = (n_req * d_mission / (math.pi * d_wheel)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    rev_ratio = n_rev / l10_rev

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(t_continuous.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 29957) < 1, "Continuous exposure should be about 29,957 h")
    check(abs(n_req - 299572) < 2, "Zero-failure missions should be about 299,572")
    check(abs(t_calendar.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 39943) < 1, "Calendar time should be about 39,943 h")
    check(abs(d_mission.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 540) < 1e-6, "Mission distance should be 540 m")
    check(abs(n_rev - 2.57e8) < 0.01e8, "Wheel revolutions should be about 2.57e8")
    check(abs(rev_ratio - 5.15) < 0.005, "Wheel total should be about 5.15 times the L10 rating")
    check(rev_ratio > 4, "Prose says the wheel total exceeds the L10 rating several times over")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    d_mission_str = fmt_length(d_mission, precision=0)
    t_mission_str = fmt_time(t_mission, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_reset_str = fmt_time(t_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_cycle_str = fmt_time(t_cycle, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    d_wheel_str = fmt_length(d_wheel, precision=2)
    t_continuous_str = fmt_int(round(t_continuous.to(ureg.hour).magnitude), commas=True)
    yr_continuous_str = fmt(t_continuous.to(ureg.year).magnitude, precision=2)
    n_req_str = fmt_int(round(n_req), commas=True)
    t_calendar_str = fmt_int(round(t_calendar.to(ureg.hour).magnitude), commas=True)
    yr_calendar_str = fmt(t_calendar.to(ureg.year).magnitude, precision=2)
    n_rev_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(n_rev, precision=2))
    rev_ratio_str = fmt(rev_ratio, precision=2)
    t_mission_h_str = fmt_time(t_mission, unit=ureg.hour, precision=2)
    l10_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(l10_rev, precision=1))
    p_fail_mission_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(p_fail_mission, precision=1))
```

The exposure wall binds even at a site requirement far looser than those rates. Suppose the warehouse mobile manipulator must demonstrate a critical failure rate $\lambda \le 1.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ failures/hour}$ (Mean Time Between Critical Failures $\text{MTBF} \ge 10{,}000\text{ hours}$) at 95 percent statistical confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$). Each retrieval mission takes $t_{\text{mission}} =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_mission_str` (`{python} MtbfCampaign.t_mission_h_str`) and covers `{python} MtbfCampaign.d_mission_str` at the `{python} MtbfCampaign.v_str` drive limit. Automated dock recharge and telemetry reset add $t_{\text{reset}} =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_reset_str`, for `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_cycle_str` per trial cycle. The drive-wheel diameter is $D_{\text{wheel}} =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.d_wheel_str`, and the drive gearhead carries an illustrative $L_{10}$ bearing fatigue rating of `{python} MtbfCampaign.l10_math` revolutions.

By the exposure wall, this target needs `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_continuous_str` failure-free hours (`{python} MtbfCampaign.yr_continuous_str` years) of continuous exposure. Discretizing this requirement into missions with per-trial failure budget $p_{\text{fail}} \le \lambda \cdot t_{\text{mission}} =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.p_fail_mission_math` requires $N_{\text{req}} = \ln(\alpha)/\ln(1-p_{\text{fail}})$, or `{python} MtbfCampaign.n_req_str` consecutive zero-failure trials. This inverts the zero-failure bound of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival at a target far beyond practical budgets of tens to thousands of runs. On a single physical rig, executing these trials at `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_cycle_str` per cycle consumes `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_calendar_str` hours (`{python} MtbfCampaign.yr_calendar_str` years) and accumulates $N_{\text{rev}} = (N_{\text{req}} \cdot v \cdot t_{\text{mission}}) / (\pi D_{\text{wheel}}) \approx$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.n_rev_math` wheel revolutions.

The wheel-rotation total is `{python} MtbfCampaign.rev_ratio_str` times the gearhead's $L_{10}$ rating, but the comparison holds only after the drivetrain ratio maps wheel revolutions to bearing revolutions, and $L_{10}$ is a population-life statistic at specified load and speed, not a destruction deadline. A campaign of this length must therefore plan maintenance and component replacement, and record each one, before it may pool trials.

In interpreting these campaigns, engineering teams must not conflate MTBF with the suite of **intervention-based physical metrics**: the Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), and Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$). In physical testing under runtime safety guardrails, catastrophic failures are prevented by permission-path overrides, emergency stops, or human safety driver interventions. What the testbed actually measures during an active campaign is the **Intervention Rate**:
$$\lambda_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{interventions}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}$$
the corresponding Mean Time Between Interventions:
$$T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{N_{\text{interventions}}}$$
and the Autonomous Completion Rate $\text{ACR} = N_{\text{unassisted}} / n$.

Conflating MTBI with MTBF is the **censored trial fallacy**. If a safety supervisor or Control Barrier Function intervened 38 times over 50 hours across 100 retrieval missions, zero hardware damage ($N_{\text{damage}} = 0$) coexists with an MTBI of $50 / 38 \approx 1.32\text{ hours}$ and an Intervention Density of $D_{\text{int}} = 38 / 54\text{ km} \approx 0.70$ interventions per kilometer. These event counts do not determine ACR: several interventions may occur in one mission, and other missions may fail without an intervention. The per-mission ledger must identify unassisted completions. Nor does zero damage estimate an MTBF of 50 hours; the report must define the failure event and account for the supervision that prevented its observation. Reset latency $T_{\text{reset}}$ adds the recovery cost to the campaign budget.

### Peak loads and unvisited conditions

The censoring built into constrained testing (@sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes) compounds the drift. Because a failed physical trial cannot be recalled (the first law of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws), safety mechanisms intervene before a failure completes, and the evidence stops where they intervene. The states a team most needs to evaluate, such as loss of traction at speed or a collision the base cannot avoid, are the states it cannot let the machine enter, because a skid into a rack damages the chassis and the sensing rig and takes the test cell offline for repair. Cages, geofences, and operators with emergency stops cut each run short at a conservative envelope. The trial records the intervention while the downstream consequence of the policy's output stays unobserved; the intervention stays in the denominator, and the consequence stays unknown.

For physical survival, a mean is an inadequate description of a peak. Consider an illustrative mobile manipulation policy with an average latch contact force of only $\bar{F} = 12\,\text{N}$ across one hundred nominal trials—well within the structural rating of the arm. Suppose its separately measured peak-force distribution instead has a 99th percentile peak impact of $115\,\text{N}$ when the gripper strikes the strike plate at a slight angular offset. That single transient impulse exceeds the shear strength of the latch pin, causing permanent structural failure despite an innocuous average.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_extreme_value_shock_sparkline.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sparkline comparing Gaussian distribution tail against Fréchet extreme value heavy tail."}
*Illustrative tail shapes motivate measuring peak forces; neither curve establishes the latch campaign's tail family or event rate.*
:::

This limitation is governed by the **physical impact roofline**\index{Physical impact roofline!definition}. When a moving arm of effective mass $m_{\text{eff}}$ strikes a rigid mechanical contact of stiffness $k_{\text{contact}}$ at approach velocity $v_{\text{approach}}$, kinetic energy converts into elastic spring deformation: $\frac{1}{2} m_{\text{eff}} v_{\text{approach}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} k_{\text{contact}} x^2$, yielding maximum elastic deflection $x_{\text{max}} = v_{\text{approach}} \sqrt{m_{\text{eff}} / k_{\text{contact}}}$. By Hooke's law ($F = k x$), the resulting peak transient impact force is:
$$F_{\text{peak}} = k_{\text{contact}} x_{\text{max}} = v_{\text{approach}} \sqrt{m_{\text{eff}} k_{\text{contact}}}$$
Because the contact shock rise time $\Delta t_{\text{rise}} \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{m_{\text{eff}} / k_{\text{contact}}}$ across rigid mechanical interfaces ($k_{\text{contact}} \sim 10^5\text{--}10^6\,\text{N/m}$) spans merely $1\text{ to }5\,\text{milliseconds}$—an order of magnitude faster than the $20\text{ to }50\,\text{millisecond}$ sensor-to-actuation loop of closed-loop neural policies—a monitor whose detection and physical response exceed that rise time cannot reduce the initial peak. To prevent permanent yield or mechanical destruction against the structural damage limit $F_{\text{limit}}$ (here the latch's `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str` threshold), physical AI systems encounter an unyielding velocity ceiling:
$$v_{\text{approach}} \le \frac{F_{\text{limit}}}{\sqrt{m_{\text{eff}} k_{\text{contact}}}}$$
As the Williams roofline model [@williams2009roofline] caps computational throughput by memory bandwidth and the kinematic stopping roofline (@sec-boundary-machine-model, @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes) caps transit speed by braking distance, the physical impact roofline caps safe approach velocity before contact. Autonomous evaluation benches cannot overcome this roofline through faster neural inference; they require either passive mechanical compliance (lowering $k_{\text{contact}}$ via series elasticity or spring couplings) to dilate the shock rise time into the bandwidth of current tripwires, or strictly enforcing pre-contact speed limits—such as the guarded approach speed $v_{\text{guarded}} =$ `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str`—before crossing the contact boundary. Extreme value theory (EVT)\index{Extreme value theory} offers candidate models for maxima, but a Gumbel, Fréchet, or Weibull family must be fitted to a defined sample of block maxima or threshold exceedances, checked against alternatives, and reported with its uncertainty; the physical mechanism alone does not select the family.[^fn-math-extreme-value] Without those data, @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails states what to measure and what protection to validate rather than predicting rare-event frequencies.

[^fn-math-extreme-value]: **Extreme value disturbance modeling**\index{Extreme value theory!physical disturbances}: The Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem describes the possible limiting forms of block maxima under stated assumptions; it does not assign a tail family to impact, glare, or latency by physical mechanism alone.

| Disturbance channel     | Peak quantity and sampling record                    | Physical consequence to test                             | Candidate protection to validate                                                  |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Compute and bus latency | Per-cycle end-to-end age and deadline misses         | Stale proposals erode braking margin                     | Freshness lease and independently timed fallback                                  |
| Contact shock           | Force-time trace, impulse, and peak at the load path | Yield or overload before a reactive command takes effect | Passive compliance and precontact speed limit; reactive limits address later load |
| Low traction            | Local friction estimate and stopping response        | Slip extends stopping distance                           | Conservative speed ceiling and tested fallback on low-grip surfaces               |
| Optical glare           | Saturation duration and perception misses            | False clearance or lost state estimate                   | Redundant sensing and independent physical constraints                            |

: **Peak-disturbance evidence and protection**: Mechanisms identify measurements and safeguards, not an EVT family or event rate. Any quantitative tail claim needs a defined population, fitted model, goodness-of-fit checks, and uncertainty. {#tbl-07-extreme-value-tails tbl-colwidths="[18,28,26,28]"}

The latch shows why the contact-shock row pairs a measurement with a protection. Each door run contributes one block maximum, its peak latch force, and twenty maxima are far too few to fit a tail that would predict how often a run crosses `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str`. A force monitor that reacts only after contact cannot undo the first peak either; its measured detection and actuator response can limit the loading that follows, while the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, a precontact speed limit, reserves the margin for the initial impact.

Distributing trials across a fleet does not buy independence. Ten machines tested concurrently in one warehouse share a production batch, a floor finish, a ventilation system, and operators trained under one protocol, so an anomaly absent from the facility, such as floor glazing or low-angle glare, reaches none of them. Ten thousand fleet hours in one facility are ten parallel observations of one narrow distribution, not ten thousand hours of independent exposure. Standardized test fixtures such as those in @fig-07-nist-test-arena buy repeatability by bounding the state space to the fixture.

::: {#fig-07-nist-test-arena fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Standardized robotic evaluation facility**: NIST response-robot test bays photographed in 2013 (Linda Joy/NIST), then described under ASTM E54.08. A zero-failure run across standardized bays establishes competence inside the arena and says nothing about glare, surface contaminants, or obstacles outside it." fig-alt="Photograph by Linda Joy/NIST of NIST response-robot test facility bays in 2013. Structured test spaces support repeatable trials within their fixture conditions."}
![](images/jpg/fig07_real_nist_test_arena.jpg){width="75%"}
:::

The repeatable challenges in @fig-07-nist-test-arena support comparisons across robotic platforms. Their controlled geometry, surfaces, and lighting also define the evidence boundary; testing factory spills, pedestrian crossings, or low-angle sunlight requires additional conditions in the campaign.

These ceilings force an architectural conclusion. Physical AI safety cannot rest on statistical confidence in the learned weights. The exposure examples at $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-9}$ failures per hour show why more trials cannot carry the whole protection argument. Runtime constraints must have their own evidence, including the assumptions under which they can prevent a hazardous action and the time available to respond. Policy trials characterize task completion and intervention rates within the tested envelope; they do not establish that the envelope will contain every fault. The protection argument therefore shifts toward the independent permission path and physical safeguards, whose limits require separate validation.

One way to establish a classical controller's stability is a **Lyapunov function**\index{Lyapunov function!stability certification} $V(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ with $\dot{V}(\mathbf{x}) \le -\gamma V(\mathbf{x})$ over a stated region, not by counting runs, and with disturbances an input-to-state stability\index{Input-to-State Stability!classical control} argument bounds the state error by the size of the input under its own model assumptions. The evaluated learned proposer carries no such stability certificate. Checking the decrease condition through its non-smooth activations is a non-convex search over millions of parameters, its latent inputs carry no physical units on which to build $V$, and contact discontinuities break the smoothness the proofs assume. Outside its training distribution a learned policy can also change its output abruptly, so that a shadow or a camera glint flips the direction of a proposed motion. The burden of proof therefore moves off the proposer and onto a low-dimensional check on an isolated microcontroller. Two strategies carry that burden, one at run time and one on the bench:

1. **Runtime Containment**: Bounding the physical authority of the learned policy by delegating the collaborative-robot force limits, kinematic acceleration limits, and emergency stops to the permission path, an independent, deterministic mechanism below the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. The protection claim then rests on the permission path and its fallback, whose state estimates, plant and actuator models, response timing, and reserved stopping margin must be validated separately from the policy.
2. **Fault Injection on Physical Benches**: Rather than waiting for passive disturbances to strike, engineers inject them. Injected trials follow the fault-injection method of @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list; their fault population belongs in a separate labeled ledger rather than being pooled with operational draws.

::: {#chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf .callout-checkpoint title="Sample size and MTBF evidence target"}

Before moving on, check your understanding of sample size scaling and physical test limits:

- [ ] **Exposure wall**: Under a stationary Poisson failure model, why does a one-sided 95 percent upper rate limit corresponding to a $10{,}000\text{-hour}$ MTBF target require `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_continuous_str` hours of zero-failure physical exposure?
- [ ] **Mechanical fatigue exhaustion**: Can you explain why wheel revolutions cannot be compared directly with a bearing $L_{10}$ rating without drivetrain mapping and load conditions?
- [ ] **Architectural containment vs. statistical sampling**: Can you explain why a task campaign needs separate evidence for runtime constraints and physical safeguards?

:::

Even under rigorous qualification protocols and automated test cells, statistical sampling alone cannot establish ultra-reliable autonomy. What remains outside any finite campaign, and which runtime monitors the record must name for it, decides how far the evidence can carry the release decision.

### Turning coverage gaps into runtime obligations

The limits of evaluation follow from the endogenous loop of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics. The states a physical campaign visits depend on the commands the permission path admitted, so no fixed dataset matches the candidate's closed-loop state distribution, and a simulator substitutes its own transition model for the plant's (formal trajectory distributions in @sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution). A simulator that models the aisle floor with the friction of clean, inspected concrete cannot show what the base does on a clear oil film, and one whose actuators respond instantly cannot show the lag of a real stator's electrical time constant\index{Actuator!stator delay}; the physical trajectory departs from the simulated one, and the departures compound into states no simulated run visited. A physical test therefore bounds only the distribution it actually sampled.

The conclusion of this particular campaign is conditional and tied to its single machine instance. A campaign that samples multiple units can support a broader declared population. The door campaign establishes that one software build on one specific hardware unit (Unit 01), from the sampled initial conditions and inside the environmental lighting and temperature present during the runs, failed with probability below `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent at 95 percent confidence. It says nothing about a colder morning that derates the joints\index{Hardware!thermal derating}, a gearbox whose compliance\index{Hardware!gearbox compliance} and backlash have grown with wear, or a displaced strike plate.

More runs on the nominal plate on Unit 01 reduce sampling uncertainty and tighten the binomial bound (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds), but they cannot reduce structural uncertainty about unmodeled physics, environmental unobservables, or hardware instance variance across the fleet. Two thousand further runs would measure that single unit with finer precision while leaving the displaced-plate cells, the loaded machine, fleet-wide unit differences, and bus jitter\index{Hardware!bus jitter} exactly as unsupported as before.

Since evaluation cannot establish how the policy behaves outside the sampled distribution, each monitorable boundary of the claim needs a runtime signal, threshold, and tested response, and the permission path must enforce independent physical constraints. Distribution support is only partially observable and an OOD detector has measurable false negatives, so conditions that cannot be sensed reliably require ODD restrictions, passive protection, or other independent barriers. The evaluation record carries these specifications in its `runtime_monitor_specs` field (@sec-evaluation-logs). The field names five monitoring channels whose coverage and response must be measured:

1. **Input Support / Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!OOD detection} Estimates whether incoming observations depart from the tested distribution using a calibrated score and reports false negatives on held-out shifted conditions.
2. **Execution Latency Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!execution latency} Measures observation age and inference duration against their separate declared limits, checks proposal renewal against the expected cadence (for example, the latch policy's `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period at `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str`), records misses, and checks that lease expiry invokes the validated fallback. A $P_{99}$ summary alone is not a hard deadline bound.
3. **Constraint Margin Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!constraint margin} Tracks the distance between the current physical state and hardware safety limits, including joint torque limits\index{Actuator!torque limit}, motor winding temperature\index{Actuator!Joule heating}, and obstacle clearance against limits specified for the hardware and stopping model.
4. **Intervention Rate Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!intervention rate} Calculates the frequency of permission-path overrides, detecting when policy instability causes excessive corrections.
5. **Environmental Assumption Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!environmental assumptions} Measures external operating conditions, such as surface traction estimated from wheel slip and ambient illumination measured by photometric sensors.

A monitor that only writes an anomaly to a log protects nothing. An invalid replacement is refused without automatically revoking a still-valid active command. When the active command's own state, evidence, or lease no longer permits continuation, the permission path acts on the actuators through a validated fallback, a speed restriction or a controlled stop, provided the sensed state, actuator capability, and reserved clearance make that response feasible (fallback logic in @sec-appendix-control-cbf). A timely, confident proposal still passes the independent state, clearance, and actuator checks before any $u_t$ is applied.

Some failures no software runtime monitor detects. This limitation constitutes the **epistemic trap of software OOD monitors**: an out-of-distribution detector operates entirely on digital sensor streams and latent representations. However, an optical illusion or sensor physics failure—such as a spotless clear glass partition, specular laser glare, or lens mud—causes the vision transformer backbone [@brohan2023rt1] to produce high-confidence, in-distribution latent feature tokens for an out-of-distribution physical obstacle. The software cannot detect what physical transduction failed to capture. A proposal can meet every deadline, respect every torque limit, and arise from apparently familiar latent features, yet steer the base directly into the glass partition; the measured clearance remains nominal until contact. Safety against such failures cannot come from statistical evaluation or software monitors alone. It requires physical zoning\index{Safety!physical zoning}, mechanical current limiters\index{Actuator!current limiters}, and independent physical safety barriers whose protective capability is validated independently of the learned model under specified physical assumptions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Physical failures undetectable by sensory telemetry are formally cataloged in @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors.
:::

These limits bind even a flawless campaign. The evidence that survives them is only as good as the campaign that produced it, and procedural and statistical errors can corrupt a campaign long before its result reaches the record.

## Empirical Evaluation Pitfalls and Metric Masking {#sec-evaluation-failure-modes}

Systematic errors undermining policy evaluation rarely stem from deliberate fraud. They arise when an evaluation protocol answers an easier question than the claim asks, creating statistical or procedural mirages that mask physical vulnerability.

### Six procedural evaluation pathologies {#sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies}

Six recurring procedural flaws distort empirical evaluation: environment selection, metric drift, test-set contamination, optional stopping, denominator filtering, and substituting demonstrations for measurements.

**Pathology 1: Environment selection.** Environment selection occurs whenever the test bench is narrower than the claim. The twenty door runs all met the nominal strike plate at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach with the base stopped and the tote rack empty. If the report states their success rate as the machine's ability to open the site's cage doors, the claim silently expands to the `{python} EvalMachine.n_absences_str` unsampled cells of the ledger and the loaded machine (@sec-evaluation-limits). Environment selection\index{Environment selection} is detected by comparing a condition ledger, which records the measured strike-plate position, approach speed, payload, and floor condition of every trial, against the boundaries of the claimed domain; a ledger that covers one cell establishes nothing about the others.

**Pathology 2: Metric drift and offline surrogate substitution.** Metric drift\index{Metric drift} occurs when the evaluation metric slides from physical closed-loop task completion toward an offline surrogate such as action agreement\index{Action agreement}, validation loss, action Mean Squared Error (MSE), or action cosine similarity against recorded expert buffers. Driven by the seductive low cost of offline compute, engineering teams substitute static metrics for live rollouts. However, as demonstrated in @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, offline surrogates produce severe ranking inversions: cosine similarity ignores command magnitude (causing static friction stalls or structural over-torque), while MSE averages across time steps and washes out non-Lipschitz contact choke points. Metric drift is prevented by mandating that the primary evaluation metrics remain closed-loop physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), with zero unmitigated tripwire crossings.

**Pathology 3: Unit-specific test set contamination.** Repeated tuning against a fixed evaluation setup creates **unit-specific test set contamination**\index{Test set contamination}. Adjusting the checkpoint or observation filtering after each batch on Unit 01 makes that robot and door part of development, not an independent holdout. The resulting improvement may depend on their particular backlash, calibration, and lighting. Audit the history of policy versions, tuning decisions, and chassis identities, and reserve fresh units and conditions for any claim that requires generalization beyond the development setup.

**Pathology 4: Optional stopping and multi-look inflation.** Evaluation protocols are equally vulnerable to unintended cherry-picking through optional stopping. When an engineer monitors a continuous sequence of physical runs and halts the experiment as soon as a target performance threshold or statistical significance criterion is reached, the reported confidence is distorted. If an evaluation team conducts an experiment where each look carries a nominal false-positive threshold of 5 percent, stopping early upon observing an apparent success across multiple evaluation checkpoints inflates the true error rate. `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_looks_str` independent 5 percent looks would have a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_any_false_positive_pct_str` percent chance of at least one false positive. Repeated looks at one accumulating run are dependent, so the inflation for a real stopping rule must be computed for that rule. Optional stopping\index{Optional stopping} cannot be detected from summary tables or final pass rates. It is detected only by auditing the pre-registered trial protocol, verifying that sample sizes, stopping conditions, and evaluation milestones were fixed before the first physical run began.

**Pathology 5: Denominator filtering and the censored trial fallacy.** A related statistical distortion occurs when the denominator of an evaluation is quietly filtered, breaking the full-denominator condition of @sec-evaluation-trial-protocol. A team that discards runs ending on software timeouts, emergency stops, sensor communication drops, or permission-path overrides as invalid test artifacts reports success over the surviving trials only. This denominator truncation systematically masks low Autonomous Completion Rates ($\text{ACR} = N_{\text{unassisted}} / n$) and artificially inflates apparent MTBI ($T_{\text{MTBI}} = T_{\text{active}} / N_{\text{int}}$). By discarding interrupted rollouts, nonzero intervention counts ($I_i \ge 1$) vanish from both the numerator and denominator, driving measured Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) toward zero. Furthermore, filtering omits the hidden operational overhead of Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)—the minutes spent untangling jammed end-effectors, clearing fault registers, and physically restoring the scene—creating a false impression of rapid, autonomous operation. If the arm opens the door on nine of ten attempts and the tenth needs an operator takeover to stop the gripper wedging against the latch, removing that attempt falsely raises the apparent success rate from 90 percent to 100 percent and reports an infinite MTBI for that batch. Crucially, infrastructure aborts—such as Wi-Fi packet drops, operating system kernel thread stalls, or bus brownouts—must remain in the denominator. The physical world does not care which software or hardware subsystem failed; an autonomous forklift that stalls in an aisle intersection because of an operating system thread lock has failed its operational mission. Removing infrastructure aborts evaluates an idealized mathematical abstraction rather than the deployed cyber-physical system. When physical constraints or safety limits truncate a run before its time limit $T_{\max}$ expires, the trial is recorded as a censored failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$) rather than omitted from the ledger. Reading survival on truncated trajectories as operational competence is the **censored trial fallacy**\index{Censored trial fallacy!definition}. Denominator filtering\index{Denominator filtering} is detected by cross-referencing low-level actuator telemetry and permission-path logs against the trial ledger, confirming that every power-on cycle, autonomy engagement, and physical reset corresponds to a recorded outcome.

::: {#ws-evaluation-nhtsa-40-percent-mirage .callout-war-story title="The 2017 NHTSA Autopilot crash rate mirage"}
**Context**: In January 2017, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) closed Preliminary Evaluation PE 16-007, which it had opened after a fatal Florida crash of a Model S operating in Autopilot mode (@sec-perception-failure-modes) [@nhtsa2017pe16007]. The closing report compared airbag-deployment crash rates in the subject Tesla vehicles before and after Autosteer was installed and stated that "the Tesla vehicles crash rate dropped by almost 40 percent after Autosteer installation," from 1.3 to 0.8 crashes per million miles.

**Mechanism**: The rate divided airbag deployments by miles driven before and after installation, and the report's own footnote noted that the rates "are for all miles travelled before and after Autopilot installation and are not limited to actual Autopilot use." The denominator therefore never measured exposure to Autosteer itself, and it was incomplete as well. A replication by Quality Control Systems Corporation found that the odometer reading at installation appears to have been reported for fewer than half of the vehicles, and that exact exposure before and after installation could be computed for only 13 percent of them [@qcs2019nhtsa]. The mileage NHTSA left uncounted, because it could be assigned to neither period, was concentrated among the vehicles with the least exposure before installation.

**Impact**: In the one cohort with complete exposure in both periods, the airbag-deployment crash rate rose 59 percent after installation, from 0.76 to 1.21 per million miles, a result the replication qualified with "if these data are to be believed." Its authors concluded that the overall 40 percent reduction was "an artifact of the Agency's treatment of mileage information that is actually missing in the underlying dataset." The replication does not measure Autosteer's effect either. It shows that the published denominator could not support the reported reduction.

**Response**: The correction came from outside the agency and two years after the closing report, because the per-vehicle mileage records that exposed the denominator were released only after a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Transportation [@qcs2019nhtsa].

**Systems lesson**: In physical AI evaluation, an unverified denominator produces a statistical mirage. Aggregating open-world mileage without engagement telemetry, operational design domain boundaries, and complete exposure records turns missing data into a safety claim. An evaluation audits the integrity of its denominator with the same rigor it applies to the failure events in its numerator.
:::

**Pathology 6: Substituting visual demonstrations for statistical measurements.** A successful video shows that the machine reached the goal under one sequence of conditions; without a sampling record, it does not establish how often that outcome recurs. Smooth $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ kinematics (rigid-body motions in three dimensions)\index{SE(3) kinematics} can conceal small physical margins. A representative campaign needs predeclared sampling from the target ODD or separate per-stratum analysis, full-denominator accounting, and a sample size tied to its stated claim.

The same discipline governs comparisons. As Jacob Cohen formalized in his statistical power analysis[^fn-math-cohen-power] [@cohen1988power], deciding whether `latch-bc-01` opens the cage door more reliably than another checkpoint requires the Type I error ($\alpha$), the Type II error ($\beta$), and the effect size, the smallest difference in success rate worth detecting. Twenty runs per checkpoint carry no stated power until those quantities and the baseline success rate are known, so the protocol fixes $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the effect size before the first run.

[^fn-math-cohen-power]: **Statistical Power in Physical Trials**\index{Statistical power!sample size}: The probability $1 - \beta$ of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. For a two-policy comparison, compute power from the baseline rate, effect size, sample allocation, and chosen test before collecting physical trials [@cohen1988power].

### Sequential probability ratio testing {#sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt}

A fixed-sample campaign can reject at its first failure, but early acceptance needs a different predeclared rule. Wald's sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) [@wald1945sequential] compares an unacceptable success probability with an acceptable one after each trial. For a strict autonomy campaign, the Bernoulli outcome is unassisted completion; for a whole-machine campaign, it is the separately declared service outcome. The same notation below can serve either test, but the outcome rule cannot change during collection.

For hypotheses $H_0: p = p_0$ and $H_1: p = p_1$, after $k$ successes in $m$ independent trials the log-likelihood score is:
$$S_m = k \ln \left(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\right) + (m - k) \ln \left(\frac{1 - p_1}{1 - p_0}\right)$$
Each success moves the score toward acceptance and each failure toward rejection. With the illustrative hypotheses $p_0 = 0.90$ and $p_1 = 0.99$, a success adds about $0.09531$ while a failure subtracts about $2.30259$. Starting from zero, an immediate failure crosses the approximate rejection boundary below; an initial success leaves the test running. This is evidence for the declared outcome, not permission to continue an unsafe physical trial.

Wald's approximate log-score boundaries are:
$$A \approx \ln \left(\frac{1 - \beta}{\alpha}\right), \quad B \approx \ln \left(\frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha}\right)$$
For standard engineering confidence parameters $\alpha = 0.05$ and $\beta = 0.10$, the decision boundaries are $A \approx \ln(0.90 / 0.05) \approx 2.890$ and $B \approx \ln(0.10 / 0.95) \approx -2.251$. At each physical rollout $m$:

1. If $S_m \ge A$: Halt testing and accept $H_1$ under the declared test (evidence for the evaluation record within the target ODD).
2. If $S_m \le B$: Halt testing and reject $H_1$ (policy rejected; abort campaign immediately to prevent hardware damage).
3. If $B < S_m < A$: Continue sampling; execute rollout $m+1$.

The approximate boundaries must be calibrated for the actual discrete outcomes and stopping rule. Ville's inequality gives a direct false-acceptance guarantee at likelihood ratio $1/\alpha$; that guarantee does not automatically apply to a different approximate threshold. The likelihood-ratio derivation, expected sample count, and overshoot treatment belong to @sec-appendix-ml-sprt. A real campaign records the hypotheses, outcome definition, calibrated boundaries, complete trace, and terminal decision in its Evaluation Summary.

The fixed-sample door campaign already supplies a useful record. A sequential design can reduce expected testing cost under its own assumptions, but it cannot repair an undefined population, a filtered denominator, or unsupported transfer to another machine.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-evaluation-fallacies-pitfalls}

An evaluation supports claims only within its tested conditions and limits. These mistakes arise when teams extend a result beyond those limits or attribute an architectural safeguard to the learned policy.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Repeated success in a single nominal condition proves broad operational readiness.*

The door campaign repeats one condition twenty times: the nominal strike plate, the guarded approach, the base stopped, the rack empty. Under the binomial model\index{Evaluation!Binomial Model}, those runs give the `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent lower bound of \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} for that condition\index{Evaluation!Confidence Intervals}, and nothing for the other cells of the ledger or a loaded tote rack that moves the arm's torque margins. Repeating the condition sharpens the nominal estimate while the deployment-critical envelopes\index{Safety!Operational Envelope} stay untested. A readiness claim must name its target ODD, allocate trials across the physical variations inside it, and report uncertainty within each tested cell. **Nominal repetition sharpens precision on a single cell; it provides zero evidence for the rest of the operational design domain.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Explicitly partition the declared ODD into a condition matrix, allocate test quotas across all operational strata, and report confidence intervals per cell rather than pooling unstratified runs.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero failures in 1,000 trials proves compliance with a 99.9 percent reliability specification.*

Suppose the latch policy opens the door `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_fallacy_str` times without a trip against a requirement of 99.9 percent success at 95 percent confidence. The observed success fraction is perfect ($\hat{p} = 1.00$), and textbook Central Limit Theorem Wald intervals collapse into the degenerate point $[1.0, 1.0]$ because estimated variance $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n$ vanishes identically. Yet exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson inversion ($p_{\text{lower}} = 0.05^{1/n}$) demonstrates that the true one-sided lower confidence bound is only `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_fallacy_str`, falling short of the 99.9 percent requirement (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds); certifying it requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs. A parallel fallacy occurs in early-stage pilot evaluation: observing zero failures in 20 trials ($p_{\text{lower}} = 86.1$ percent) cannot certify even a 90 percent reliability target ($n = 29$ clean runs required), let alone an industrial 99 percent reliability target ($n = 299$ clean runs required). The gap is an evidence deficit, not an empirical proof of compliance. The trial budget follows strictly from the claim and confidence level, fixed in advance, and the report must state the exact Clopper-Pearson lower bound rather than the perfect empirical fraction. **Zero failures with an insufficient sample size represents an evidence deficit, not an empirical proof of compliance.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Reject asymptotic Wald intervals at parameter boundaries; precalculate the required sample size via the non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson bound ($n = \lceil \ln\alpha / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$) or the Poisson Rule of Three ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), and report exact one-sided lower confidence bounds.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *High offline action agreement on static logs guarantees closed-loop physical stability.*

An evaluation report that cites close agreement with expert actions\index{Evaluation!Action Agreement} on recorded runs—such as negligible action MSE, high discrete token accuracy, low validation perplexity, or high action cosine similarity—has measured dataset imitation on frozen buffers and nothing more. The aisle policy of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics matched its recordings almost exactly and still spent its side clearance through the kinematic integration of a persistent heading bias. Covariate shift\index{Evaluation!Covariate Shift} adds a separate risk when the resulting states leave the demonstrations. Furthermore, at non-Lipschitz mechanical contact interfaces, sub-millimeter errors that barely register in MSE trigger destructive reaction forces ($F = k \Delta x$) and mechanical jamming, producing severe ranking inversions where low-MSE policies fail while higher-MSE policies succeed. Similarly, action cosine similarity discards command magnitude entirely; a policy predicting an action in the correct direction but with 20 percent insufficient torque stalls against stiction, while 20 percent excess torque triggers joint tripwires. Offline surrogates can screen candidate checkpoints before physical trials, but a claim of closed-loop stability\index{Control!Closed-Loop Stability} rests solely on closed-loop physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) counted against the full denominator. **Offline validation loss, MSE, and cosine similarity measure dataset mimicry; closed-loop physical dynamics decide survival.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Treat offline loss, action MSE, and cosine similarity strictly as preliminary screening filters; require closed-loop physical rollouts with full-denominator accounting as the sole empirical evidence for policy stability.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Peeking at accumulating rollouts and terminating testing early inflates false safety certification.*

An engineering team halts after 30 clean runs because the accumulating result looks favorable, then reports the confidence of a fixed-sample test. That stopping rule changes the test; its error rate cannot be read from a fixed-sample calculation. A predeclared zero-failure protocol may stop at a failure to reject the candidate, but early acceptance needs its own calibration. Sequential probability ratio testing supplies one such approach. Ville's inequality ($P(\sup_{m \ge 1} L_m \ge 1/\alpha \mid H_0) \le \alpha$) controls false acceptance at its stated likelihood-ratio threshold; approximate Wald boundaries require their own error calibration. **Choose the stopping rule before collecting outcomes, and report the error guarantee for that rule.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Pre-register sequential decision boundaries ($A \approx \ln((1-\beta)/\alpha)$, $B \approx \ln(\beta/(1-\alpha))$) and update the likelihood-ratio martingale after each rollout, halting testing only when cumulative log-likelihood crosses an absorbing threshold.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Crediting the learned policy with surviving transport stalls that the enforcement architecture handled.*

The mobile manipulator completes 50 nominal aisle runs, and the team credits its learned policy with tolerance to SerDes bus jitter\index{Hardware!SerDes Jitter}. A qualification test then injects a mailbox stall that outlasts the chosen `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences. The lease\index{Safety!Freshness Lease} expires, and the permission path detects the stale lease and initiates a controlled dynamic stop, analogous to a Category 1 stop\index{Safety!Category 1 Stop}, from the fallback ladder of @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. That response comes from the enforcement architecture; nominal completion records do not establish that the neural weights detect or compensate for the stall. Fault injection\index{Evaluation!Fault Injection} must measure the permission path's detection and stopping behavior against the available stopping distance margin, and the evaluation report must attribute the protection to the hardware mechanism that supplied it. **Do not credit unverified neural weights with safety guarantees provided by the deterministic permission path.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Conduct systematic fault injection (injecting communication stalls and sensor dropouts) to independently benchmark the permission path's stopping envelope, and attribute safety mechanisms strictly to the hardware and software layers that executed them.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero physical collisions or hardware damage in testing proves high autonomous policy reliability.*

When an autonomous vehicle or mobile manipulator completes an extended campaign with zero collisions, teams frequently declare that the policy achieved high reliability (e.g., claiming an MTBF equal to total run time). But if human safety supervisors or runtime Control Barrier Functions intervened repeatedly to prevent impending impacts, the system achieved zero hardware damage ($N_{\text{damage}} = 0$) only because the protective safety envelope intervened to censor the failure trajectories. What the testbed actually measured was an intervention event; the true autonomous reliability is captured by Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR) and Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI). Frequent human takeovers can make a proposed service impractical, while frequent automatic least-change adjustments may be normal operation; the report must separate those classes. Discarding these interventions or treating them as unassisted proposer successes confuses the protective competence of the safety architecture with the operational competence of the learned policy. **Zero collisions under active safety supervision must be interpreted alongside interventions; they do not by themselves establish policy reliability or complete protection coverage.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Enforce full-denominator accounting; record every supervisory takeover, CBF clamping event, and tripwire crossing as an autonomy failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$), and report those strict autonomy measures beside whole-machine task completion, cycle time, and protective outcomes.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Qualifying a policy on a single reference robot assumes zero unit-to-unit hardware variance across the fleet.*

An engineering team executes 300 failure-free runs on a single robot (Unit 01) and declares the policy qualified for fleet release. When flashed onto Unit 02, the policy repeatedly jams or chatters. Mechanical tolerances in harmonic drive gear teeth ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$), structural link compliance under load, camera bracket mounting angles ($\pm 0.5^\circ$), and stator winding resistance tolerances ($\pm 5$ percent) alter the plant transfer function across physical chassis. Testing on a single golden unit measures that individual unit's specific mechanical quirks, not fleet-wide reliability. Furthermore, testing at a single time of day ignores environmental unobservables—such as diurnal solar glare angling through clerestory windows, changing floor friction from ambient humidity, or motor winding heating ($I^2 R$)—that shift physical dynamics without changing a single neural weight. **Evaluating a single robot chassis characterizes that specific unit's mechanical quirks; fleet release requires stratifying trials across the manufacturing distribution.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Stratify physical qualification across multiple chassis serial numbers drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, audit unit-specific backlash and kinematic offsets, and quarantine final qualification testing to fresh units that were not used during policy development.

:::

## Summary {#sec-evaluation-summary}

Closed-loop evaluation measures the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol, so a success rate describes a declared population rather than a weight file. Because the machine's own admitted actions choose the states it reaches, which is Part II's endogenous-data principle, only trials that close the loop through the permission path measure what the proposer does; open-loop scores cannot see the drift those actions produce. A zero-failure confidence limit then bounds the sampled population under its sampling assumptions, and censoring at the edge of safe operation keeps that population inside the envelope the campaign could afford to enter. More trials narrow that bound without widening the population, and the exposure wall places rare-hazard rates beyond any campaign a physical machine can run.

The door campaign shows the shape of the claim that survives. Twenty clean runs support a lower confidence limit for the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, with the base stopped and unloaded, and nothing about the displaced-plate cells the demonstrations never covered or about the loaded machine. The coverage gap catalog records the conditions no trial visited, and assigns them to independent physical constraints and a feasible fallback on the permission path rather than to the proposer, because a runtime OOD detector can miss what it has never seen.

The stipulated recovery branch shows how this boundary can expand. Fresh experience supports a changed candidate, and independent nominal regression and displaced-plate qualification support the new record. The initial archive is not a permanent ceiling on future competence.

The chapter's product is the evaluation record—the Evaluation Summary contract of this book's lineage—and four of its parts travel forward:

1. *Bounded operational claim:* The target ODD\index{Operational design domain!target ODD}, inside the policy manifest's declared ODD, where performance was empirically characterized.
2. *Reproducible configuration and ledger:* Digests of weights, firmware, and calibration, with unit-specific hardware tolerances and every attempted, aborted, and overridden trial kept in the denominator to derive honest physical metrics ($\text{ACR}$, MTBI, $D_{\text{int}}$, $T_{\text{reset}}$).
3. *Coverage gap catalog:* The known absences of the data and the manifest's omission log, plus the conditions and hardware units the trials left unvisited.
4. *Runtime monitor specifications:* For each boundary that can be sensed, the signal, threshold, and tested response that the permission path must implement at runtime\index{Runtime monitoring}.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Closed-loop evaluation and reliability"}
* **A success rate belongs to a population**: The rate reflects the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol. More runs tighten uncertainty within the sampled conditions; additional hardware units and operating conditions require evidence of their own.
* **Choose the regime for the question**: Replay screens prediction and computation, simulation probes modeled feedback, shadow operation measures execution on live inputs, and constrained physical trials expose real interaction. Each leaves a different gap; their results cannot be pooled as interchangeable trials.
* **Completion and intervention answer different questions**: ACR measures unassisted task completion, while MTBI and intervention density expose the burden of each declared intervention class. Whole-machine task completion and protective outcomes remain separate. Reset latency reveals the recovery cost. Retaining every attempted run prevents protection supplied by supervision from being credited to the policy.
* **Clean runs still leave uncertainty**: Twenty clean trials yield a one-sided 95 percent success lower limit of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent under iid sampling. The target and confidence determine the trial budget; predeclared, calibrated sequential rules can support early decisions without choosing a favorable stopping point afterward.
* **Rare hazards require independent protection evidence**: Feasible campaigns cannot supply arbitrary amounts of failure-free exposure. Runtime constraints and physical safeguards therefore need separate validation of their sensing, response, and fallback assumptions; a good policy score cannot supply that evidence.
* **The record carries capability and limits**: The Evaluation Summary states what the proposer accomplished within its target ODD, preserves the complete ledger, and identifies unsupported conditions. Its monitor requirements guide runtime design, while unmonitorable gaps remain restrictions on the operational claim.
:::

The endogenous-data principle makes the evaluation record conditional. A run of incident-free trials samples the states the admitted actions reached; it neither covers every reachable state nor proves that hazards exist beyond the sample. The engineer must carry both the measured competence and the remaining uncertainty into runtime design. The Evaluation Summary makes that handoff explicit through its target operating domain, coverage gaps, and monitoring requirements. Part III builds the sensing, state estimation, and permission mechanisms needed to act within those limits; their integrated verification follows before a release claim can rely on them.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From evaluation records to perception"}
Part II ends with a record that confines trust in the learned proposer to its target ODD and names the runtime monitors the rest of the machine must supply. Part III builds the runtime that meets those obligations. The first of them falls on perception, because an input-support monitor or a latency monitor can act only on observations that carry their capture time, their coordinate frame, and their uncertainty. @Sec-perception follows a measurement from the sensor to a spatial claim that the permission path can date, place, and bound before it permits motion.
:::

```{=latex}
\part{key:vol4_runtime}
```
